speechtext:
1.	In fiscal years (a) 1988-89 (b) 1989-90, did any multicultural or minority rights organizations apply for funding from the Department of Justice and, if so (i) what number (ii) did any actually receive funding and, if so, what number (iii) were any applications received from Quebec and, if so, what number (iv) were any granted and, if so, what number?
2.	In fiscal years (a) 1988-89 (b) 1989-90, were any projects dealing with human rights or legal aid funded (i) in Canada (ii) in Quebec and, if so, what number?
3.	Were any applications for funding of such projects received and, if so, what number?
4.	Has Justice Canada taken specific steps to comply with subsection 3(2) of the Multiculturalism Act and, if so, what steps?
5.	Has the Minister of Justice entered into any agreement or arrangement with any province respecting the implementation of the multiculturalism policy in Canada, as per subsection 6(2) of the Multiculturalism Act and, if so, has there been any agreement or arrangement respecting multicultural legal aid services?
6.	According to the Operation of the Canadian Multiculturalism Act Annual Report 1988-89, the Department of Justice "has committed funds for four major conferences in 1989-90, each of which will include exploration of issues relating to multiculturalism"; were these conferences planned or held and, if so (a) what were they (b) in what locations were they held?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: MIDDLE EAST REQUEST FOR AUTHORITY TO TRAVEL
speechtext:
1. The question refers to "multicultural or minority rights organizations". This term is unclear and has been defined broadly to include all organizations applying for funding in the area of multiculturalism or human rights in order to provide a more complete answer.
No statistics are kept regarding the type of information requested in this question and so all numbers have been manually determined and are approximate.
a)	In 1988/89, 49 aplications from such groups or for such projects were received, including 9 from Quebec. Twenty-one projects were funded, including 4 from Quebec.
b)	In 1989/90, 33 applications were received, including 7 from Quebec. Twenty eight projects were funded, including 7 from Quebec. In many instances applications were received in one fiscal year and approved for funding in the following fiscal year.
2.	In answering this question and the next question, human rights has been broadly defined in order to provide a clearer answer.
a)	In 1988/89, 33 projects dealing with human rights or legal aid were funded by the Department. Of the 33, 9 were located in Quebec.
b)	In 1989/90, 37 human rights or legal aid projects were funded in Canada, including 10 from Quebec.
3.	In 1988/89, the Department received 68 proposals dealing with legal aid or human rights. In 1989/90, 42 proposals dealing with legal aid or human rights were received by the Department.
4.	Yes. The Department has taken action during the past years to meet the objectives of the Act. Specifically, programs and activities were undertaken in the following areas:
(a)	Human Resources Management
-By developing a three year employment equity plan to improve the participation of visible minorities in the department's work force.
(b)	Communications
-By increasing Employee Awareness of the Act and Canada's Multicultural, Multiracial Diversity through internal communications.
-By portraying in communications materials Canada's multicultural and multiracial diversity.
-By the use of languages other than French and English, in accordance with the Government Communications Policy.
(c)	Funding Initiatives

-By funding research and education centers, workshops, conferences and courses with a multicultural and minority rights groups component.
-By continued funding of the Canadian Judicial Centre, the Public Legal Education and information (PLEI) agencies and legal aid under the Criminal Legal Aid Agreements with provinces and territories.
-By holding a seminar to sensitize all funding officers to the Multiculturalism Act and multiculturalism aspects of funding.
(d)	Research
-By conducting research to enhance access to justice for multicultural groups.
(e)	Service to the public
-By continued adherence to Guidelines for the Representative Depiction of Ethnic and Visible Minorities and Aboriginal Peoples in Government Communications.
-By the use of languages other than French and English, in accordance with section 13.2.4 of Government Communications Policy.
-By distribution of materials through the mail and/or through attendance at multicultural and multiracial groups' conferences.
5.	No. The federal-provincial cost-sharing agreements for adult criminal and young offenders legal aid services provide for uniform, mandatory coverage to ensure equal treatment in cases covered by the agreement, namely, all serious offenses and those in which loss of liberty or livelihood is likely; the provincial agency will determine the financial circumstances under which an applicant for legal aid may be approved as a recipient.
All applicants charged with an offence covered by the agreement and who meet the financial eligibility test must be approved as an applicant regardless of their ethnic background or cultural association, and the cost of services provided is shareable under the agreement.
The presence of well established legal aid clinics throughout Canada, including areas where various ethnic groups are predominant, assures that legal aid services are accessible to all Canadians.
6.	In 1989/90, the Department of Justice provided funding for the following conferences:
The conference entitled "Realities and Needs for the 90's" was sponsored by the National Council of Jamaicans and Supportive Organizations in Canada, Inc. It was held in Toronto on May 19-20, 1989, and included the participation of human rights organizations, youth groups, social development agencies, NGOs, etc.
The conference included workshops on the following topics: literacy; economic development; institutional participation; the Canadian justice system and minority rights; youth; housing; and the aging visible minority population.
The Conference entitled "Human Rights in CrossCultural Perspectives"-University of Saskatchewan, College of Law, was held in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan from October 12 to 14, 1989.
The National Conference on Racial Equality in the Workplace-Faculty of Business, McMaster University in conjunction with the Hamilton and District Chapter of the Industrial Relations Research Association, was held in Hamilton, Ontario from March 2nd to 4th, 1990.
The conference entitled "The Contemporary Women's Movement in Canada and the United States: A Retrospective and Prospects for the Future", Centre for American Sudies and Centre for Women's Studies and Feminist Research at the University of Western Ontario was held in London, Ontario from May 3rd to 5th, 1989. This conference included a major session on "Racism and the Women's Movement".

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question? The hon. member for Northumberland.

Mr. Speaker, today I rise to continue debate on the motion relating to the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq. I must say to begin with that it is with dismay and great trepidation that I rise as the member of Parliament for Northumberland to debate this issue.
I have been devoted for most of my life to non-violence, have advocated non-violent resolution to problems, and now represent a constituency in Canada, a country which at this present time is close to open warfare in the Middle East. This puts into jeopardy the lives of many Canadian men and women, each one whose lives are sacred to me, each one of those people who right now with our Armed Forces are very important to me, each one who are as a sister, a husband or a wife to me. It is with great trepidation that I rise in the House to present my views on the government's action and inaction, and to express my concerns about the motion on the floor of the House today.
September 27, 1990

First, I cannot accept that our government sent Armed Forces into this crisis in the Middle East without recalling Parliament so that we could have full debate on the issue and an understanding of what the circumstances are in the Middle East. I also condemn the fact that the Government of Canada sent our forces into the crisis in the Middle East two weeks in advance of any UN resolutions which would have required their presence there. Rather, we sent forces into the Middle East crisis in response to an American request.
In terms of the motion that is before the House today, I cannot deny for a moment that I support fully the first comments in the motion which are:
That this House condemn the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq and, encouraged by the unprecedented international consensus demanding the immediate and unconditional withdrawal of Iraqi forces from Kuwait and the full restoration of the legitimate government of Kuwait, affirm unequivocally its support for Canada's actions in the United Nations Security Council and its support of all relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions adopted since August 2-
That, I support fully.
I have to say at the outset that I have the highest regard and respect for Canadian Armed Forces now serving in the Middle East or who have served in the past in other areas of the world, and the greatest respect for those many people in Canada who have lost their lives in serving the cause of justice and freedom on behalf of all Canadians. But I am quite alarmed that the purpose of our Canadian Armed Forces seems to be changing radically from that which Canada has represented in the past decades.
It is ironic that yesterday here on the Hill we had the unveiling of a statue of a very highly respected Prime Minister, the Right Honourable Lester B. Pearson, a man who won the Nobel Peace Prize, who was present when the United Nations came into being, who was so outspoken in support of this country being involved in dialogue to resolve crises world-wide, and who made this nation so respected in our peacekeeping role. Suddenly, it seems to me that we are diverting from this traditional role in Canada and that we are willing to set that aside, become regressive and take on an offensive role.
Our government has not done sufficient to carry on a process of negotiation to try to bring the crisis in the Middle East to a peaceful resolution. Lives of Canadians are being put in jeopardy.
Government Orders
To describe in some detail what I am referring to, I think it is important that Canadians understand that in the Middle East presently there are two operations in place. The Americans have two different strategies for resolving the crisis which are being hotly debated in the United States. Again, as I say, Canada has two possible positions, one to maintain our traditional role in peacekeeping and being strong advocates as negotiators, or the role of going in, forgetting about strong diplomacy and negotiating positions, and being prepared for offensive action.
In terms of the operations in the Middle East, I totally support our Canadian Armed Forces, with all of the skills they have, and their presence in the Middle East to support United Nations resolutions. From that perspective I can support the role of our Armed Forces, the three ships and equipment, and the CF-18s that are in the area, so long as they are employed only to support UN resolutions.
The second operation that is taking place in time in the Middle East is as a result of Saudi Arabia and Kuwait calling upon governments around the world, Under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, asking for nations' support in resisting further invasions by Iraq, particularly into Saudi Arabia. The U.S. and over 26 other countries around the world, now and over the past weeks, have been building up troops and military equipment deterring aggression but also putting us in a very vulnerable position in terms of an unplanned offensive act on the part of any of the participants. The activities and build up of those troops and equipment on the Saudi Arabian border are not as a consequence of any UN resolutions but they put us in a very volatile situation, one which puts at risk Canadian lives if there is one mistake. I believe that we, as Canadians and as Parliamentarians, should have had the opportunity to debate more fully exactly what the strategy of Canada is in this crisis and to have urged, as is our traditional role, much more dialogue and negotiation as a process to bring about peace to the Middle East situation.
Personally, I cannot support any action on the part of our government which directly numbers and counts the loss of Canadian lives in the strategy. I believe that the strategy of peacekeeping is no less difficult and requires no less strength than that of offensive military action. I believe that the difference between the clenched fist and the open hand exists in the mind of the person who holds

September 27, 1990
Government Orders
that hand. But I believe that the same strength of conviction, determination and skill is required from both postures and I believe that traditionally Canada, with the skills of our armed forces which cannot be surpassed, I do not believe, by any force anywhere in the world, that our position has been to offer the open hand of negotiation and peace and not the clenched fist. That is what I will personally support.
In the motion of the government, I believe that the government does not give through that motion the necessary respect to our forces supporting only UN resolutions, but leaves a door open for our troops to become engaged in conflict beyond anything envisioned through the UN resolutions at this point in time.
I understand from the speeches that have been given on the other side of the floor that the Canadian forces are present in the Middle East under Canadian command. I believe, given the risk and the insecurity that exists in the situation in the Middle East at this time, that there should be a UN command for the forces in the area. If that is difficult to achieve, we should at least have a joint command in that area so that there is a co-ordinated effort in the area come whatever may come. I certainly pray to God that we can resolve the situation in the Middle East peacefully.
I also believe that if you look at the past history and the recent past history of what has happened in the Middle East, we as Canadians bear responsibility for some of what is happening today. It has been known to us that during the eight year war between Iraq and Iran that Saddam Hussein of Iraq used chemical warfare against troops in that war. In fact, we know that he used chemical weapons against his own Kurdish population within the country of Iraq.
I do not believe that we did everything possible to stand up and condemn those transgressions of all international law. As well, we have been aware of many other human rights abuses in Iraq and in and about the Middle East area. And yet, we have continued to benefit, as a nation, from arms sales to that area.
At the present time in our world's history, we are seeing many precedents being set. We have the end of a cold war, which we all welcomed, and we see in the Middle East crisis new alliances which we would never have imagined possible. We must be doing everything
possible to support the United Nations in a process of condemnation of Iraq for its activities and in trying to improve what has been accomplished today by the United Nations through the resolutions that have been supported in relation to the Middle East crisis. We are all encouraged by what has been achieved so far in that forum and we must do everything possible to protect that process and enhance it.
I believe by expressing support for actions outside of UN resolutions, we set the foot for destruction of what has been achieved to this point in time by the United Nations. Alliances could change very, very quickly in the Middle East if conflict were to open up. I think that we set ourselves up for a holocaust of proportions that we do not want to imagine and that I personally cannot countenance. As a Canadian member of Parliament, I believe that every life is important, particularly Canadian lives, but the lives that have been lost already as a result of this man who runs the regime of Iraq are also important to me.
The lives of everybody involved in a conflict in the Middle East are important to me and we must focus constantly on the faces of those people who are in the region, who are there to protect our peace and our democracies and systems of government that represent the peoples of the world everywhere. We must be aware and conscious of the importance of those people's lives, their dedication to maintaining peace on our behalf. We cannot become involved in a conflict whereby we can start counting how many lives we are willing to lose in order to achieve other objectives. I believe that it is possible, but it is not easy with our forces there who are prepared to maintain a peacekeeping role. It is important to achieve the same objectives through dialogue and negotiation and peacekeeping that is possible. I believe it is more possible to achieve those objectives than it would be through open conflict and warfare.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore have to say that I support totally the amendment proposed by the Liberals on this side of the House that says yes, we do support Canada's role in enforcing United Nations resolutions, but we censure the government for not recalling Parliament at the earliest opportunity to fulfil its legitimate function of consultation and debate as to what role Canada should play in the resolution of the present crisis and that upon adoption of this motion the said motion shall be deemed

referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Northumberland on a very thoughtful intervention. I share many of the concerns that she raised in the course of her remarks.
I want to ask her a question with respect to one of the longer term issues that obviously has to be addressed in the course of resolving the tensions in the Middle East. It goes without saying that the immediate priority is to seek the enforcement of United Nations resolutions calling for the unconditional withdrawal of Iraq from Kuwait and an assurance that security will be maintained in that region.
Obviously though, one of the long-term questions that has to be addressed is the very difficult and tragic plight of the Palestinians. Of course, this has been exacerbated by the events in Kuwait resulting in some 40 per cent of the resources which would normally be sent to support the people of the West Bank and Gaza being cut off. So, it is a desperate situation.
We know as well that unfortunately Israel has stepped up its campaign of harassment and violence in that region. We have seen the bulldozing of homes and shops in the Gaza. We have seen the refusal to reopen universities on the West Bank and Gaza.
I would like to ask the hon. member what her views are with respect to the importance in the longer term of responding to this crisis as well as part of a regional solution to reduce conflict in the area, and very specifically, whether she agrees that there must be an international conference in the region, which would include representatives of the Palestinians or the Palestine Liberation Organization, which has been recognized as their representatives, an international conference which would deal with the claim of the Palestinians for self-determination which may include a state and which would finally resolve this historic and tragic grievance of the Palestinians in that region. Does she support this as part of an over-all comprehensive approach to the situation in the Middle East?

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying in my comments, I believe that right now there is an unusual alliance of interest in the conflict represented among the Arab nations themselves. Also, on the international scene, we are seeing alliances that we would never have dreamed of even a year ago.
As I was saying, I believe as well that if we were to get into open conflict, we would put those alliances that exist right now in support of peace in the world in jeopardy, because there are so many unresolved issues in the Middle East. One that my colleague raises is the situation of the Palestinians in the Middle East.
Yes, I believe that we must do everything possible as a nation, and we must be more aggressive in trying to promote peaceful negotiations and dialogue to address the issues of the Palestinians and the state of Israel, and all of the many other very difficult historic problems in the Middle East region.
Before the Middle East crisis erupted on August 2, it was the intention of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade to look carefully into the situation as it exists and to analyse the situation in the Middle East before this crisis.
I think it is important that our committee continue to look at and try to investigate so that Canadians can understand just what the problems and positions are of the different parties to all of the conflicts in the Middle East.
I think there has been trepidation on the part of Parliament to discuss these issues in the past. Without discussion, without witnesses coming before us to explain the various positions that exist, we will never be able to take an effective role in trying to resolve the issues of the Middle East.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to that exchange in this debate, it sounds like the position of the Liberal Party may very well be in keeping with the honourable traditions established by former Prime Minister Mackenzie King, which would be stated a conference as necessary but not necessarily a conference.
That is not the point I wish to pick up from what the hon. member for Northumberland has said. I listened to her speech and I found it a very heartfelt speech. There are a lot of points I would like to pick up, especially when she talks about an historical perspective and this whole role of peacekeeping. In the next few moments I want to concentrate on peacekeeping, Canada's role as a peacekeeper in the international community and the United Nations.
Perhaps, even following the hon. member's example, we could go back and look at some history. I will go back even further than the recent history to which she referred. I was reading very early yesterday morning a
September 27, 1990

passage which pertained to a Canadian by the name of Stephen Leacock who in 1913 was expressing his fury. He was furious when the Liberal dominated Senate killed the Conservative naval bill which would have provided the money to build three dreadnoughts as an emergency contribution to the British navy.
It almost begins to seem that there are just a very few pieces on the Canadian political chessboard. Whether it is 1913 or 1990, we are still involved with whether the Liberal dominated Senate is going to kill a Conservative bill. In this case another element has to do with three Canadian ships being deployed on an emergency basis, or in that case money provided for their purchase as part of an international peacekeeping effort. Indeed there are many parallels.
That case in 1913, just as the debate we are having now, followed two years after a hard fought election on the issue of free trade with the United States or, as they called it in those days, reciprocity. Here we are many years on and we might well ask: Is there progress?
To come to the present and think of just yesterday afternoon when the statue to former Prime Minister Lester Pearson was unveiled here on Parliament Hill, we can reflect that through his person we see epitomized in fact some of these steps of progress, because he was very much identified with the formation of the United Nations and particularly, for which he was recognized with a Nobel Peace Prize, the role in the Middle East in dealing with the Suez and at that time a new role for the United Nations as a peacekeeper. That brings us again to this theme that I want to explore more: Canada's role as a peacekeeper whether it is in the Middle East or elsewhere, but in keeping with the debate today, most assuredly in the current crisis in the Gulf.
At the end of the First World War, the nations of the world created the League of Nations. At the end of the Second World War, the countries of the world created the United Nations. Now, at the end of the cold war, what are we creating? This is in fact our moment of history. What I think we are creating or have the potential to create is a new world order that coincides and completes the dream, the spirit, and the words of the United Nations Charter, words and the spirit that were
Government Orders
confounded during the long twilight years of the cold war.
When I was a student of international law at the University of Toronto, and after that when I was studying international law at the Academy of the International Court in The Hague, what really came to impress itself on me was the realization that we cannot genuinely have international law until we have international law enforcement.
For a moment let us consider this proposition in its domestic context to drive the point home. I think all of us feel that Canadians are peaceable people and that we are generally law-abiding. I can remember living in Montreal at the time of a police strike in that city. I think it could have been any other city in Canada as well; let me make that very clear. As there were no police forces, the principal streets in Montreal were turned into drag strips, the traffic lights meant nothing, store windows were smashed, there was looting and so on in Canada's premier city.
That was convincing evidence once again that although 99 per cent or more of Canadians are routinely law-abiding, there are always some who are willing to push beyond the limit and to take advantage of the fact there is no one around to enforce the laws, laws formed by consensus that are necessary for the maintenance of domestic peace, order, and good government.
I do believe profoundly that the same applies on the international level. Until we have international peacekeeping forces of a permanent and standing nature, an international police force, international law will lack the essential element of any law and that is the ability to see that it is obeyed. We are not starting on this from scratch.
I referred earlier to the work of Prime Minister Pearson. His contribution was to introduce a new notion about peacekeeping in the Suez context and, in keeping with the UN charter, to see the deployment of military forces from various member countries of the UN, under the blue flag of the UN, into the situation to assert the military force behind international law and order.
We have seen that example. We have seen the most acute example of military action being taken in the case of Korea. However, generally something that all Canadians are proud of is the fact that there has not been a single United Nations peacekeeping operation in which Canadian Armed Forces personnel have not participated

September 27, 1990
Government Orders
or, put positively, we have been there every time there has been a role for a United Nations peacekeeping force.
As I said earlier, it is after the cold war, we see a consensus among nations and, this is our moment of history. In the debate on Monday the hon. member for Waterloo pointed out the following:
For many years in the time of the East-West confrontation we have looked at a standing UN peace force. There have been designs and models and because of the East-West confrontation we have not been able to move.
He urged that we try to establish the machinery for a UN standing peace force with battalions held in reserve by national governments so that in an emergency, such as the current one we are debating or any other regional conflict, the United Nations and Canada as member of the United Nations would not be beholden to any one major power, formerly called superpowers, to act and take a leadership role.
I believe that this is truly the opportunity for us to look at new possibilities and seek a Canadian role to advance this concept of a standing United Nations peace force, just as we have within the respective countries of all member states domestic peace forces.
Certainly the unprecedented situation in the gulf crisis shows that we do have a truly united nations effort going on there. There are 158 countries that have come in, in support of the actions being taken by the United Nations.
Just briefly but for the record, I think it is important to note what those resolutions are. They seem to increase as each day goes by. We are now at the stage where eight resolutions have been passed by the Security Council of the United Nations concerning the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq.
On August 2,1990 Security Council resolution No. 660 condemned the invasion of Kuwait. On August 6, resolution 661 instituted sanctions against Iraq and occupied Kuwait. August 9, resolution 662 condemned the annexation of Kuwait by Iraq. On August 18, resolution 664 called on Iraq to allow other nationals to leave Iraq and occupied Kuwait. On August 25, resolution 665 authorized the use of reasonable force to inspect shipping and
ensure that the sanctions outlined in resolution 664 were in fact being respected.
On September 13, resolution 666 set out the conditions under which humanitarian shipments of food and medicine could be made to Iraq and occupied Kuwait. On September 16, resolution 667 condemned Iraq's incursion into diplomatic premises in occupied Kuwait- I would note that that included premises of the Canadian mission there-and the detention of diplomatic personnel. On September 25, resolution 670 was adopted limiting air transport into Iraq in furtherance of the sanctions.
Never in peacetime has any countiy, which has violated international law the way Iraq has, faced such a solid wall of sanctions. Many of us have looked at previous examples of the use of sanctions and felt that it was a flawed instrument, an effort that was often circumvented and of very little effect. Certainly in this case the United Nations support-and I mean the 158 or so countries of the United Nations that are behind these eight Security Council resolutions-indicates that this very serious situation is being well handled and the aggression that was anticipated has to date been contained to the invasion of Kuwait.
Any suggestion that Canada's actions in the gulf crisis have been contrary to our tradition as peacekeepers reflects an opinion that has been overtaken by the facts. This is both peacekeeping and peace making. That is theme I want again to emphasize as we now look at the new possibilities in the post-cold war era of finding co-operation to make the United Nations all that it was dreamt it could be in 1945.
Peacekeepers have traditionally been deployed under the United Nations flag between the parties to a conflict following a truce. Certainly in the case of the current conflict, Canada would support the placing of peacekeepers between Iraq and Kuwait once Baghdad withdraws from the countiy it has invaded.
This also raises other questions that I do not have time to go into now, but one must contemplate the nature of a liberated Kuwait. Speaking for myself, I would hope that we would be supportive of democratic forces in Kuwait so that in the future the people of that countiy would have the opportunity to really have a representative and democratic countiy.
September 27, 1990

The sending of Canadian sailors and ships, of Canadian aircrew and aircraft to deter this aggression and to enforce the UN sanctions that I have referred to is also peacekeeping. It is as much peacekeeping as having Canadian soldiers wearing the blue beret of the United Nations in Cyprus or anywhere else around the globe. Our naval and air forces and the forces of a number of other countries are there under explicit UN auspices.
I listened to the member for Northumberland talking about when forces were deployed and when resolutions were passed and I understand the narrow points that are being made. She also asked whether Parliament was or was not recalled soon enough. I do not want to debate that, I am simply saying that when taking a broad view of Canada's role as a peacekeeping country and as a peacemaker, we must go beyond the small details and look at the broad outlines of what is happening. I think it is a very significant moment in world history as we pursue global peace to see this concerted action by so many countries, not only Canadians, but the people of Bangladesh putting their armed forces in harms way.
This drawing of a line is indicating to the Saddam Husseins of the world that international boundaries are to be respected and that the united nations of this world will not tolerate armed invasion and occupation of independent countries.
Our commitment to peacekeeping is and must remain unshakeable. In these difficult days, as we consider our future as Canadians and what the new constitutional arrangements will be for our country, the essential thing is to focus on the values that really make us all Canadians and that do unite us as Canadians. One of those, most assuredly, is the value of peace and the honourable and sometimes very costly tradition of maintaining peace even when that requires the deployment of Canadians who proudly wear the uniform of our country.
Our contribution to international order, not only through United Nations peacekeeping forces, but our overseas assistance, our diplomatic initiatives and so many other roles that are part of this proud tradition is now coming into a new phase, a new era. It is not one where anyone can state, with certainty, what will be, but certainly we can outline what the goals ought to be and work towards those.
Government Orders
It is certainly something that other countries recognize in us as Canadians. Whether it is this current situation in the gulf, whether it is Central American governments designing a peace plan and getting support and assistance from Canada, whether it is our involvement with Japan who is developing its own new interest in this area, whether it is our efforts with Namibia turning it into a new country and a member of the United Nations from having been the last colony in Africa and making it become fully a democratic country, or whether it is the parties to the Cambodian conflict finding where we have provided valuable suggestions for monitoring and upholding international peace there. This is the point. Canadians are committed to peacekeeping and peace making. International order, respect for sovereign countries and the rule of law depend on it.
I hope that we can find here in Canada, just as Lester Pearson found in the fifties in the Suez crisis, a new dimension, an additional forward step in defining and in defending the role of peacekeeping. We must work toward a United Nations standing peacekeeping force to continue through the long and difficult months that will lie ahead. The resolve must be there, not only in goods times of peace but in times of bleak and difficult challenge like this, when Canadians have to be sent into areas to support the principles and the spirit of the United Nations to see that we truly have the rule of international law.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to have a discussion with the parliamentary secretary, and I thank him for outlining the government's position. Perhaps he and I, unlike the NDP, can stay on topic. He probably notices that every time the NDP do not know what to say, they find another topic because there are some areas such as foreign policy to which they cannot contribute. I certainly hope in the next few years they will be able to understand the world a little bit better than they have shown in the past.
We are trying to get straight answers.

Straight answers? If you had a question about the subject, you would get a straight answer. I am sure the new critic from British Columbia will be spending a lot of time in the library in the next period getting caught up on world affairs.

Government Orders
The parliamentary secretary suggested that the issues raised in the speech of the member for Northumberland were nuances in the debate and not central to the point. I think they are central to the point. I think Parliament has a very important role to play in Canadian foreign policy. We have a long tradition of having good discussions on foreign policy and there is a goodwill among Canadians that we do the right thing. Whether it is in areas of human rights, peacekeeping or dealing with nuclear disarmament, this House has spoken at times with one voice to ensure that Canada proceeds in the proper way.
The absence of Parliament sitting during the summer was not just a minor nuance to us but in fact is central to our criticism of what the government is doing and central to our criticism of the motion.
Perhaps the parliamentary secretary could elaborate on why the government has not been more insistent that the command of this military operation-because it is a military operation-is not more directly in the hands of the United Nations. We have, as a middle power, consistently taken the position that it is organizations like the UN which have to be the vehicle for keeping peace. Although we appreciate the speed with which people have to respond to the crisis with the dangers that are there-and nobody kids themselves about that and the goodwill with which we have supported the United States-the point still is that other countries turn to Canada to make sure that organizations like the United Nations are front and central in these missions.
It seems to me that the government could have done more to ensure that the United Nations was in control of this particular operation. I would like the parliamentary secretary to explain exactly why this was not done and what efforts will be made in the future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not refer to any nuances in the speech of the hon. member for Northumberland. I said I was concentrating on the broad lines of what is happening in historical patterns and that I did not seek to enter into a debate as to the chronology of certain events or the timing of the debate within Parliament. However, I welcome the question of the member from Winnipeg. He and I studied questions of international relations
when we were both students at Carleton University, it seems just the other day. In fact, it was in the mid-60s.
I want to pick up on this point about the current initiative of Canada in relation to the United Nations. First, the Prime Minister, in his discussions with the President of the United States as this matter developed during August, played an important role in driving home the point to the American government that any action they took in the region ought not to be a unilateral American initiative but rather ought to be a United Nations enterprise. I think this is something that has not been known generally, but it is a fact that this was a very important effort and those of us who recognize how the United States responds in international crises would detect over the long view of history a tendency to go in alone and deal with the situation according to American interests.
The Prime Minister, and I say this very proudly, displayed a good use of his good relations with the American president in urging that this become a United Nations initiative.
I would also draw to the attention of the member from Winnipeg, in case he was not here to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs speaking on September 24 in the House, a quote from page 13246 of Hansard:
We have encouraged our close allies, we have encouraged others, and we have used our influence and our position on the Security Council to ensure that the action that proceeds is action that is within the mandate of the United Nations and, indeed, that the mandate given by the United Nations expands to take account of the circumstances as they develop in the region. We are working very hard to have United Nations' auspices respected.
That was a statement in the House on Monday by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Further in reply to the member, our Minister of National Defence also said in the House of Commons on Monday that both the Departments of National Defence and External Affairs, and I quote from page 13261 of Hansard:
-are working toward and imploring the United Nations to put a blue flag over the whole of the multinational effort.
Certainly Canada wants this to be and be seen as a United Nations effort. That is the whole thrust of Canadian foreign policy. It is consistent with the policy of previous governments and I am sure will be the policy of future governments of our country. We were there at the creation of the United Nations. We are there now at this time of testing for the United Nations. We want to see

this continue under the blue flag and with the blue beret of the United Nations in this area.

Mr. Speaker, I want to pick up on the last point with which the parliamentary secretary dealt with respect to the assurance that Canada is playing an active role at the Security Council in an attempt to bring this operation in the Middle East under effective United Nations command.
I know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated that he was urging the United States not to take unilateral military action in the region but rather to ensure that any additional moves that are taken are within the context of United Nations.
Given the fact that the subamendment which my colleague, the leader of the New Democratic Party, moved urges this House to agree "that Canada work at the Security Council to seek assurances that no country will undertake offensive military operations against Iraq unless they are under UN command and explicitly authorized by the Security Council".
I would hope, given the assurance of the parliamentary secretary, that in fact he would be prepared to indicate that he and his colleagues are prepared to support this subamendment since this is precisely what has been indicated as the government position at the United Nations.
I would like to ask the parliamentary secretary whether, indeed, he does support the thrust of the sub-amendment because, as I say, it indicates that Canada would work toward this as an objective.
Second, I would like to ask the parliamentary secretary the same question I asked the member for Northumberland. I know he will not give us a Mackenzie King answer because he has just condemned that. What is the position of the Government of Canada with respect to a longer term regional resolution of the very serious questions concerning the situation of the Palestinians in the Middle East? Does his government support the convening of an international conference with the participation of all affected parties in the region, including the Palestine Liberation Organization? If so, is he prepared to make a commitment that Canada will work toward achieving this objective?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway on his recent appointment to the position as External Affairs critic for his party and answer both his questions, dealing with the last one about a conference first.
Yes, we would support the holding of a conference in the region to bring the outstanding issues to some resolution. We think it is important that the representation of those attending such a conference be equitable. We think that the agenda for the conference ought to be clearly defined in advance of the meeting taking place so that there can be a fairly specific indication of the issues to be dealt with and the approach to them.
As to the timing of it, this would obviously be determined by the judgment of a number of players in the region, a number of countries and the United Nations, as to what would be the appropriate time to get this under way. Speaking for the Government of Canada, it is our view that the earliest possible opportunity should be seized for this.
The situation with which we are preoccupied involves primarily a military confrontation, but Canada has never pursued its role as a peacekeeper simply in one dimension. We have sought, apart from any military role, the two other avenues of diplomatic initiatives and overseas financial assistance and development programs and so on. On the diplomatic side Canada is quite open and would be supportive as to how this could be done. I think that is a clear statement of the government's policy.
With respect to the resolution that is before the House and the New Democratic Party's subamendment to it, I agree with the NDP critic that the general spirit of what is there is consistent with what I have been saying. I recognize the sometimes devious nature of the hon. member in trying to deal with parliamentary points. Everyone understands that when resolutions are drafted and amendments proposed to them, there is some effort to catch members in an awkward position where they may have to vote against their own views or the policy of their party. This is something that is understood as parliamentary games. Consistent with what I said to the hon. member for Northumberland, I do not want to deal with it on that level. I am trying to look at Canada as a peacekeeping country and where we can go in the broad

September 27, 1990

terms of the foreign policy of our country in dealing with this.
To complete, in answer to his question-and it is really further as well to the hon. member from Winnipeg- what kind of role and what kind of say Canada has in a situation like this directly depends on how prepared we are to be there, contributing. Unless we have Canadian forces in the situation, we cannot expect to have a voice in the situation.
Canada is respected internationally because in the past we have been present and accounted for. In the past when Canadians have had to make sacrifices to be part of some effort internationally, to respect peace and international law, those sacrifices and the blood that has been spilled by Canadians are the price for us having a voice and respect internationally today.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in the debate on this very important question, and specifically on the government's motion.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to stress that the New Democratic Party fully supports the condemnation of the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq, as well as the rest of the resolution which states, for example, that "encouraged by the unprecedented international consensus demanding the immediate and unconditional withdrawal of Iraqi forces from Kuwait and the full restoration of the legitimate government of Kuwait," the House affirms "unequivocally its support for Canada's actions in the Unites Nations Security Council".
Of course we support these principles set out in the motion, as well as "all relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions adopted since August 2".
Mr. Speaker, the problem we have is with the part following that. The part about supporting without restriction "the dispatch of members of the Canadian Forces to take part in the multinational military effort in and around the Arabian Peninsula". That specific part is the one we have a big problem with. The government of
Canada always took the position that collective action under the United Nations, as integral part of our foreign policy, is the best way to ensure lasting international peace and security.
However, Mr. Speaker, recent decisions made by the Conservative government in response to the Gulf Crisis take us far away from this basic Canadian foreign policy principle that a great many Canadians agree with.

As I said, I want to make it very clear that we join in the unreserved condemnation of the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq. We fully support the United Nations resolutions which have been adopted to respond to this aggression on the part of Saddam Hussein.
As well, I want to note that Canada's response has not been in the traditions of this country. Indeed, that started with the failure of the government to recall Parliament to allow parliamentarians to debate this very important decision to send troops into the Middle East to the gulf at the earliest possible opportunity.
During Question Period on Monday, I reminded the House of the fact that in August 1988, when the government sent peacekeeping troops to the Iran-Iraq border following the cessation of hostilities on that border, that the then Minister of National Defence indicated: "When such a major new undertaking is given, I have a moral responsibility to report to the people's representatives to ask for their support."
That moral responsibility has been completely abdicated by the government. We can certainly contrast this, as other members have pointed out, with a decision to recall Parliament in August of 1987 to deal with 174 refugees arriving on the shores of Nova Scotia. There was no hesitation to recall Parliament then.
Indeed, many other jurisdictions and Parliaments were recalled by their governments, including the British Parliament, to deal with this crisis in the Middle East. We condemn the failure of the government to recall Parliament at the earliest possible occasion to ensure that we would have an opportunity to speak and that our voices might be heard before the decision was finally made to send our troops into the Middle East. We recognize very clearly that this is simply a continuation of
September 27, 1990

the old manipulative style of politics that we have seen too frequently from the government.
This was the first opportunity, following the end of the Cold War, for Parliament to debate on an early occasion what our response might be in this very serious issue of the crisis in the Middle East. I suggest that the government failed this first test of foreign policy.
I would note as well that our military responsible was not made pursuant to any United Nations request or, indeed, under United Nations command. We recall that the day after of the invasion the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that Canada would not be involved militarily in the gulf crisis. A couple of days later, the Prime Minister met with President George Bush. Four days later, before any United Nations resolution had been adopted, he announced, that Canada would be sending three ships to the Middle East.
It was not until two weeks later that United Nations Resolution 665 was adopted which authorized enforcement action. It had the very limited purposes of enforcing the sanctions agreed upon by the United Nations.
There is no question that current United Nations resolutions do not in any way authorize the massive military build-up which has occurred in that region. There is no UN command structure. There is no overall UN co-ordination of military activities in the region.
There was an alternative. Canada could have played a role in leading the world, along with like-minded nations, in ensuring that this operation did come under effective United Nations command and co-ordination. There are mechanisms in the United Nations Charter, under Article 42 and other articles, to ensure that the United Nations would be in charge.
As well, there is the military staff committee of the United Nations. This a body which admittedly has not been active over the years, but this could have been an opportunity for the military staff committee to play an important and effective role in ensuring military co-ordination of this operation.
We must also note-and many Canadians have expressed concern about this-the hypocrisy which has too often characterized the American response to these questions. For example, the Americans are now wrapping themselves in the United Nations flag. We welcome
Government Orders
the United Nations role that has been played, but it was just a very short time ago that the deputy representative of the Americans at the United Nations was saying that he looked forward to the United Nations leaving New York. He said he would bid a fond farewell as it sailed off into the sunset. As well, we know the Americans are behind in their contributions to the United Nations by some $750 million. It is interesting to note this newfound support for the United Nations, and it is one that we welcome, but it is certainly not coincidental that it comes at a time that it is in the American interest as well.
I would have hoped that the Americans would have called for the enforcement of other United Nations resolutions affecting that region as well, including Resolution 242. We have heard nothing from the Americans calling for effective enforcement of United Nations Resolution 242 which calls for Israeli withdrawal from the occupied territories in that region as well. A double standard has been in force for some time.
Where was the effective international action when Iraq invaded Iran in 1980? Where were the sanctions? Where was the world condemnation at that point? Where were the sanctions and the effective international action by Britain the United States against South Africa which occupied Namibia for over 40 years? Where was the effective international action following the Iraqi gassing of Kurds resulting in thousands of deaths in March 1988? Where was the condemnation of American aggression in areas such as Grenada, Libya and Panama? Mr. Speaker, there has been a double standard and I think that we must point that out in the response of the world to this crisis.
As well, it is important to note that the nature of our involvement in the peacekeeping operation has changed substantially since the initial debate took place on this question. When troops were first deployed to the region on August 10, Commodore Ken Summers, who was one of the military commanders, stated that Canadian ships and the helicopters they carry would be operating beyond the range of Iraqi missiles and aircraft in the Gulf of Oman. At some point that mission was changed Now we have our ships and their personnel and troops going right into the heart of the Persian Gulf. Of course, they

Government Orders
need air cover. That is why a squadron of CF~18s has been sent.
We must ask ourselves, why have they been sent, not just to the Gulf of Oman, but right into the heart of the Persian Gulf? Who made that decision? Why was it made and who is, effectively, commanding our troops in the region at this time? What happens if the Americans decide to launch unilateral military action against Iraq or, indeed, if another jurisdiction such as Israel decided to launch a pre-emptive strike, the kind that has been suggested, for example, by Henry Kissinger or, a surgical strike as he called it, on Iraq. The potential consequences for our troops in that region could be absolutely devastating. Yet there is no effective United Nations command.
As well, I would note that unfortunately the peace dividend, which so many of us have been looking forward to, resulting from the end of cold war hostilities, may be squandered as a result of this new action. Unfortunately, we know that the arms merchants are always looking for new areas to sell their wares. Indeed, the arms merchants were active in supplying Iraq for many years. Of course, George Bush has already indicated that Operation Desert Shield is going to be used as an excuse to increase substantially his military budget and seek support for funding for Star Wars and other military buildup.
Canada's longstanding reputation for peacekeeping is exemplified by our involvement in UNIIMOG, the United Nations peacekeeping activity on the Iran-Iraq border in 1980, which is continued, risks being diminished by our military response to this crisis in response to American requests and not under UN supervision. I suggest that there was a different way that Canada could have at the outset offered to be available for a peacekeeping role when needed. We could have offered substantially increased resources to assist in the repatriation of refugees in that area.
We know the devastating plight of tens of thousands of refugees who are streaming out of Kuwait, people from Sri Lanka, Pakistan, the Philippines and other countries. We know the impact that this is having on those people and on their families as well that they were supporting through the money that they sent home. We know that this is having a veiy serious impact on the Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza who were supported, as some
40 per cent of their income came from remittances from Palestinians working in Kuwait.
Canada has offered resources. I welcome the commitment of the government of $75 million in resources to assist those states that are particularly hard hit, but much more could and should be done.
As well, we must assess the impact of this crisis on prairie grain farmers. They may very well need additional compensation. That is something that we are going to have to look at carefully. I know that my colleague, the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre, has addressed and will continue to address this issue on behalf of prairie farmers. In the year leading up to June 30, 1990, Iraq was in fact Canada's largest customer for wheat, at 721,000 tonnes.
As my leader indicated, we want to pay tribute to the troops who are in the region under very, very difficult conditions, to the embassy staff who have worked so hard, again under unprecedented difficulty. We want to express particularly our concern for the Canadians who are still in the region and for their families at home who are obviously suffering a great deal from this situation. Where do we go at this point? What are our recommendations to the government at this point? First of all, as our subamendment indicates, we believe very strongly that Canada should be playing a leadership role within the context of the Security Council to ensure that this operation comes under United Nations command and United Nations co-ordination to ensure that in fact there is not unilateral military action taken by any state, whether it be the United States or elsewhere.
We must note as well that of course there are other agendas in this debate. We have seen oil companies in too many instances making windfall profits. I would suggest that the government look at the possibility of a windfall profit tax. Why should the oil companies be able to profit from this crisis? Why not ensure that those excess profits are taxed and perhaps put them into a fund to assist the refugees in the region. We know that the Americans do have strategic interests in the region. They want to ensure a continued supply of cheap oil. They have wanted for some time to establish a military base in Saudi Arabia.
I think we have to ask, among many questions that must be asked, what concrete evidence was there to suggest that in fact the massive American build-up in Saudi Arabia was necessary to in fact deter a possible attack on Saudi Arabia. We are looking at concrete

evidence. What was the concrete evidence suggesting that such an attack on Saudi Arabia may have been imminent?
We should give sanctions an opportunity to work effectively. They are going to have a serious impact on the Hussein regime. Iraq stands to lose over $19 billion per year. They rely on imports for 80 per cent of their basic materials. They are dependent on the sale of oil for over 95 per cent of their export earnings. We suggest that our ships should go no further, should have gone no further because I believe they have passed the Straits of Hormuz now or they are in the process of doing that. They should have gone no further than the Gulf of Oman. We should have invited United Nations observers on to our ships. We should have, again, played a key leadership role in ensuring that all foreign armed forces in the area come under effective United Nations command.
We should be doing far more to assist those countries that are particularly hard it. We heard from the President of Zimbabwe yesterday. Sixty per cent of their oil comes from Kuwait. There are other countries as well that have co-operated in sanctions that are hurt particularly hard. I am thinking of Egypt, Jordan, Turkey and others such as Romania which have played an effective and important role in enforcing these sanctions. I hope that Canada together with other countries can in fact assist in reducing the hardship.
Mr. Speaker, I know that I just have a couple of minutes left and I want to close by talking about the longer term approach that Canada might take in resolving this crisis. First of all, as I say, we did have an option. We had an option to operate within the framework of the United Nations, to recall Parliament early and that was not done. Instead, we are seen, I fear, by too many countries as having responded, whether it be to George Bush, Secretary of State Baker or to NATO, instead of within a comprehensive and clear United Nations framework.
I hope that the subamendment which we propose with respect to an assurance that no country will undertake offensive military operations against Iraq unless they are under United Nations command and explicitly authorized by a resolution of the Security Council that will be adopted that will bring about enhanced support for the repatriation of refugees in the area as well as those
Government Orders
countries and areas that have suffered, including the occupied West Bank and Gaza and, finally, that there will be effective leadership in reaching a long-term solution that includes ending the possibility of chemical or nuclear warfare in that region. That has got to be done.
We are are talking about all states in the region, Iraq quite clearly, Libya, Israel, other states. There must be effective international assurances controlling the flow of conventional arms. We have been dumping arms into that region for years. We must move toward a just distribution of wealth, respect for human rights and democracy. Many of the nations in this region have been condemned for serious breaches of human rights. We must reduce western dependence on fossil fuels and promote conservation and alternative energy sources. Of course, we must convene an international conference which would include all parties affected, including the Palestine Liberation Organization, to facilitate the right of Palestinians to long overdue justice and self-determination.
I would hope we can still, even at this late date, change our policy as a nation, show effective leadership within the context of the United Nations and make all Canadians proud of our re-establishment of that traditionally respected role of leadership and not be seen, regrettably, to once again be following American leadership as opposed to international leadership in world affairs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Patrick Boyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a comment or two.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway, who is the NDP critic, has singled out a number of points in his exhaustive remarks, and in response I should like to raise just one or two points. My first point has to do with the chronology of events.

The member was condemning Canada and urging a change of our policy because of, as he put it, following the United States. Canada was not following the United States. Canada was consistent with our traditional policy which I would argue is consistent. Just for the record, when the New Democratic critic said that our action was

Government Orders
taken before these resolutions of the United Nations, I had already read into the record this morning, and I will repeat, that it was the August 2 UN resolution which condemned the invasion of Kuwait. It was the August 6 UN resolution which instituted sanctions against Iraq and occupied Kuwait. It was August 9 which condemned the annexation of Kuwait by Iraq. It was August 10 when Prime Minister Mulroney announced the intention of the Government of Canada to respond to this crisis by deploying the three ships, the Athabaskan, Terra Nova and Protecteur to the region, and announcing at that time that with the understanding that it would take time to prepare the ships to sail and time additionally to arrive there that there would be opportunity for the debate which we have been having here since Monday on this issue.
I think that it is important that the condemnation that is being made of our government should at least try to be factually based. The government does not apologize for the swiftness of the response to this crisis. The fact is that efforts at the United Nations, and generally through the international community, were moving in tandem. I hope, although he only confined himself to discussing future possibilities in the last several moments of his speech, he could in his response pick up, for example, the point I was outlining about having a United Nations standing peacekeeping force, some of these ideas. Let us, on something as important to this country and this world as this current crisis in the gulf, try to stop scoring parliamentary points and look at the broad outlines of what is possible for future Canadian policy.
I would welcome the response of the critic for the New Democratic Party on some of these future actions because I know in bringing to this subject his concerns, he will want, as all of us will, to look ahead to the future and try and see beyond an attitude about the Americans or the Soviets or anyone else in the region, that we look here at what we are doing as an independent country, a charter member of the United Nations, seeking, in a difficult circumstance that to date is being well managed, to find a positive role to ensure that the peace that is tenuous but is still holding can in fact be held.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the hon. member's question. I am sure that it was inadvertent but, of course, in his chronology he overlooked a very fundamental point. While the resolutions to which he referred which were adopted by the Security Council prior to August 10 in fact did impose sanctions, it was not until August 25 that the Security Council adopted a resolution which in fact authorized the use of minimal force to enforce those sanctions.
It was the meeting of the Prime Minister with the President of the United States, George Bush, on August 6, followed by a meeting of the NATO countries on August 10 in Brussels, which led to the decision to send troops. That decision was not just pursuant to the United Nations-and indeed it was not pursuant at that point to any United Nations resolution, because it was not until two weeks later that the United Nations authorized that; fortunately most other countries that have troops in the region now did in fact wait for the United Nations-but rather it was for the second mandate.
It is often overlooked that there are two different mandates that this government is operating under. One is purportedly under the United Nations, and indeed at this point under the United Nations, but the second is this vague mandate of deterring aggression which is completely separate from the United Nations mandate. I would hope that the parliamentary secretary would recognize that and recognize that as of August 10 there was no United Nations resolution authorizing the use of force or troops to enforce sanctions.
The hon. member suggests that we look to the future and to what role the United Nations might play effectively. I agree completely with him. I certainly welcome the suggestion of a United Nations peacekeeping force. I think that is a very positive suggestion and one that I hope Canada is actively pursuing in the Security Council.
However, I remind the hon. member-and I would welcome his comments on the point-that there exists now a body under the framework of the United Nations, and I am speaking of the military staff committee, which is in a position to move and to co-ordinate, particularly under articles 42 and 43 of the charter, military action by the United Nations. Is Canada actively pursuing this
September 27, 1990

option within the framework of the United Nations as well at this time?

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very attentively to the hon. member's speech. I congratulate him at the outset on being made external affairs critic for his party. I understand he has been relieved of his responsibilities as justice critic and is now taking on the onerous responsibilities as external affairs critic. I may say that his speech sounded rather like that given by a Secretary of State for External Affairs, because it was very difficult to tell what the position of the party was having listened to the speech.
Secretaries of State for External Affairs are known for their obfuscation and coverup of clear positions, because they do not want to make it appear that anything they are doing is too dramatic. I can recall even some Liberal Secretaries of State for External Affairs who were known for that. The Hon. Paul Martin when he was a member of the House-and I am not referring to the present member for LaSalle-Emard; I am talking about the former member for Essex East-was well known for the statements he made.
I recall a comment made by some persons who were sitting in the gallery of this House. They were from the United States and unfamiliar with the workings of the Canadian Parliament. They thought they had been in a church when they left having listened to a speech given by the former member for Essex East. The hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam. Do I have the constituency correct? He reminded me of the same when he was giving his speech a moment ago.
Burnaby-Kingsway.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Burnaby-Kingsway, I am sorry. I did not mean to accuse the other hon. member of the same party of making such a pious speech.
I was surprised at the suggestions in his speech that somehow Canada was going to be involved in offensive military operations against Iraq. It is not the expectation here that the forces there are going to used for offensive military purposes. It is designed to bring to an end to the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq which has so outraged world public opinion. What I could not understand from the hon. member is-perhaps I am simplifying things-that I think he said he supports the presence of the troops there nowthat they are under some kind of United
Government Orders
Nations mandate. He did not before because they weren't, which I think is clear, and we agree with him in that respect. He seems to be saying that he does not want the troops to be involved in offensive operations, which we would agree with. We do not particularly want offensive operations there either.
What are they supposed to do? Is he saying that they should withdraw if offensive operations get under way? Is he saying that if there are offensive operations they are to be managed by the United Nations, which I think he was saying? Is he saying that somehow the United States which has the bulk of the troops there should manage any offensive operation under United Nations auspices? Is he saying that the United Nations should appoint somebody else and operate offensively, or is he saying the United Nations should appoint somebody to operate the entire force there in a defensive way?
I do not know what he is saying. I found it very difficult to follow that part of his speech. I wonder if he could clarify what role it is he expects the Canadians forces there to fulfil, or does he want the Canadian forces to withdraw?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member's time for questions and comments has expired, but do I have unanimous consent to allow the hon. member to reply to the question?
Agreed.
Absolutely.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member has accused me of being somewhat obfuscatory in my speech, I must say that was the most bizarre, meandering, obfuscatory question I have ever been posed.
Our position in respect of the use of offensive military action is very clear, and certainly I will be pleased to reiterate what that position is. Our troops that have been dispatched should clearly only be operating under the auspices of United Nations resolution 665 for the purpose of enforcing sanctions.
They should go no farther than the Gulf of Oman. I made that clear. Perhaps the hon. member was involved in researching some arcane procedural point at that particular part of my speech, but our troops should go no farther than the Gulf of Oman. They should be there, as

September 27, 1990
Government Orders
I say, for the purpose of enforcing that United Nations resolution.
We have said as well, quite clearly, that there should be no offensive military action taken by any state in the region without United Nations sanction, explicit sanction by the Security Council, and that that should be under effective United Nations command.
That is the subamendment which we have tabled. Perhaps the hon. member has not discovered the Order Paper yet, but if he would read the Order Paper he would find our position very clearly set out in the subamendment.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words, I suspect very brief words, with respect to the motion before the House which is condemning the action and the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq, supporting Canada's actions at the United Nations and the resolutions by the Security Council, and supporting the dispatch of Canadian forces to the Arabian peninsula.
This is a very severe crisis not only for our country but for the entire world. It is a very frightening one with all of the implications it brings with it not only as a result of this unprovoked invasion by Iraq and the threat of Iraq's forces going farther than into Kuwait but carrying on into Saudi Arabia and perhaps even beyond that, but it brings with it as well all the potential horrors of possible chemical warfare. Certainly it would appear to be a long, drawn-out conflict, a long, drawn-out blockade with the efforts to impose sanctions, whether by sea, by air or over land.
Obviously it is going to have very severe economic effects on countries around the world, particularly on some of the countries in eastern Europe which are now struggling to get on their feet after the forces that have been enveloping them recently have loosened their bonds. Communism seems to be disappearing and democracy and a free market system seems to be taking place. Obviously all of this is going to impact on those countries very severely, particularly countries like Poland, Hungary, and Czechoslovakia.
However, with all this great crisis, it seems to me there are some very encouraging bright spots in the whole situation. There are at least three as far as I am concerned. The first of those is the fact that nations around the world have united and come together in an effort to deal with this unprecedented and unprovoked
aggression by Iraq. We now have something like 26 nations involved in this process. I think that is extremely encouraging. It is not just a process involving one or two. It is not a process involving North American nations or NATO nations alone. A vast number of nations around the world are now joining together to resist this aggression.
Second, another very bright light is that for the first time that I can certainly remember-and I suspect the first time that most of us can remember-the United States and the U.S.S.R are both on the same side. They are both taking the same position. They are both co-operating and both doing it in a spirit aimed at trying to promote some sort of world peace and order in opposition to unprovoked aggression.
Third, as far as I am concerned the brightest light of all is the fact that this is taking place under the United Nations. Albeit, notwithstanding the comments of my hon. friend and other members in this House, this is an action which does involve the United Nations. It is sanctioned by the United Nations and is proceeding as a United Nations operation.
In my view it is part of a developing process that I hope will go to the ultimate extent of providing some sort of world order and policing body, which will be able to intervene very quickly, more quickly than we have been able to do so in this situation where we are confronted with unprovoked aggression and similar situations such as we have here now.
With respect to the United Nations, I think it is important for all of us to realize that the United Nations has been a very-I hesitate to use the word useless-ineffective body in the last few years and for a long time. When it was born during and at the end of the Second World War, it was bom with a feeling that here was the great hope for the world, that suddenly we would have some form of world government developing in which we could maintain some sort of world order and rule of law. That did not materialize.
It is like all institutions and, if we look at our own British parliamentary system, that has been an evolutionary process that has taken place over hundreds and hundreds of years. I suspect that the evolution is still taking place. Each step along the way is another step which reinforces and makes it more difficult to go back to the things we have had before. I see this, in that light, as an extremely positive step leading toward something

that will be of benefit not only to Canadians but to all the citizens of the world.
I believe this is something that is consistent with positions that Canada has taken in the past. It is true that some of them were positions of peacekeeping roles to maintain order along a green line in Cyprus or some sort of line of cease fire, truce, or whatever. However, there was also the precedent of the Korean War situation in which Canada participated under the United Nations flag in a very positive way.
All these things are developmental stages toward a very effective United Nations. I think that is an extremely bright spot and one that I welcome.
I have heard a great many comments, concerns, and criticisms about the way this situation has been developing. I hope I have a minute or two to comment on some of those.
The first is that in some way this is a double standard because the United Nations and other nations around the world did not react to other events, other unprovoked aggression, in a similar fashion in the past. That may be very true, but we have to start somewhere. Surely we do not say that this is horrible because we are starting now to react to a situation. We also did not have the United Nations and the U.S.S.R. acting together in the past either. Now we do have. Again, this is part of an evolutionary process.
