Mr. Speaker, there is an Indian myth about a tribe, starving, unable to track the mighty buffalo herds. Two children brought the hunters robes made of coyote skins, begging that they wear them. Some hunters laughed, some were angry with the children's interference.
However, two elderly, wise members of the tribe agreed to put on the robes and in doing so, found they had the vision of the coyote and were able to direct their people to the buffalo.
Mr. Speaker, many stories of The Great Medicine Wheel teach an important lesson-that to live in harmony and well-being we must see with the eyes of others, hear with the ears of others and speak with the tongue of others.
The challenge now is for all hon. members of this place to see and hear and thereby better understand the commitment of Canada's first people.

Mr. Speaker, prairie grain producers face historically low prices owing to reduced world demand and highly subsidized grain exports by the European Economic Community and the United States.
The result is that Canadian elevators and terminals are plugged and producers, through no fault of their own, cannot sell any grain. Their only source of cash is the advances which they obtain at the elevator on the strength of their farm stored grain. While producers have no opportunity to market their grain, they have, at the same time, borrowed to the hilt for chemicals, fuel and other inputs.
In the circumstances, I call on the Minister of Agriculture to waive, for this 1990-91 crop year, the interest requirement on at least the first $30,000 to $50,000 of cash advances per individual producer. This will provide some immediate cash flow for farmers who cannot afford to pay any more interest at this time.

Mr. Speaker, one lesson that the Oka imbroglio has taught us is that all Canadians must be treated with respect. That is what the First Nations demanded and that is what all of our ethnic communities want.
In respect of this point, I call upon the federal cabinet to listen to the voices of Afro-Canadians and review the CRTC decision of August 8, awarding the last available FM licence in Toronto to country music interests rather than to Milestone Communications Limited, a black-owned and operated firm which seeks to air black music and reflect black interests.

Mr. Speaker, with the appointed Liberal majority in the Senate intent on killing Bill C-62 many Canadians have already begun to ask, where do we go from here?
Killing the GST will not solve Canada's economic and structural problems, yet our Liberal colleagues offer no alternatives. Seemingly we can no longer expect them to do so. If they were, would they be taking this action, which amounts to no more than simply a partisan statement. If they were, would they not be worried about the costs and fiscal responsibility? Mr. Speaker, Canada Post continues its dictatorial ways as the corporation strips rural Canada of its postal services.
After October 15, 1990 rural P.E.I. will no longer enjoy Saturday mail delivery. This reverses Canada Post's 1982 position which acknowledged that the island was in a unique situation.
After October 30, many rural post offices will suffer severe reductions in business hours. The Richmond post office, for example, will be closed from 11.30 to 1.30, the busiest time of the day.
The elimination of Saturday rural mail delivery will cost Canada Post Corporation almost $200,000 per year in net revenues which is contrary to their government mandate, force newspapers to set up their own rural distribution routes, thus dramatically increasing subscription costs and generally limit mail service to rural residents of P.E.I.
The reduction of operating hours of rural post offices will reduce their revenue generating capacity, thereby ensuring that they will not be able to operate economically. This will give Canada Post an excuse to close these post offices.
Mr. Speaker, I call upon the government to summon Canada Post before the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations to account for their actions.

September 27, 1990

Mr. Speaker, once again we have seen women become victims of the Canadian justice system as well as victims of violence. The judge and prosecution in a sexual assault trial allowed two years of delays so that a police officer who had drugged and sexually assaulted a 19-year old police cadet would get his pension. The officer pleaded guilty after 15 court appearances and can now collect $130,000.
Two Ontario crown attorneys have said judges are biased against women in sexual assault cases after a judge handed a suspended sentence to a man who had sexually assaulted a 13-year old girl.
If the government believes as I do, that this is completely unacceptable, it must negotiate with the provinces to ensure that judges receive mandatory education on the issues of violence against women and on women's equality.
It must ensure that all Canadian judges receive this training as they are appointed to the bench and judges who are already there must also receive this training.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like most other Canadians I have watched with strong feelings the face-to-face confrontation between the army and the Mohawk warriors at Oka.
Considering the incredible tensions and passions, the presence of so many weapons on both sides, the incredible pressures on all involved, and the army of media throughout the situation, I am amazed and relieved that those involved were able to show tremendous restraint and avoided using those arms which could only have resulted in death and injury. In my view the army handled this unprecedented situation in the best possible manner under strained circumstances.
I want to thank Chief Lawrence Paul of the Millbrook First Nations for helping me understand the concerns of the natives throughout the situation. I look forward to working with the chief as we address the outstanding issues in the future.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was appalled by last night's chaotic end to the Oka stand-off. Was it really necessary for the army to fix their bayonets? Was it really necessary to shove women and children to the ground? Those scenes were disgraceful.
This crisis has focused national and international attention on aboriginal issues. The government must now deal with those issues quickly, honestly, and fairly. The Minister of Indian Affairs has said that once the guns were down, the disputed land would be turned over to the Mohawk people of Kanesatake. We expect this to happen without delay.
We also expect real action on the Prime Minister's new aboriginal agenda. The agenda is long on promises, and short on specifics.
Fundamental changes to current policies are needed. To show its goodwill the government should immediately announce that it will no longer require aboriginal people to extinguish their rights in claims negotiations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this weekend the Prime Minister will go to New York to co-chair the World Summit for Children.
While there, it is expected that he will reaffirm Canada's commitment to ratify the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, obliging Canada to comply with the terms of the Convention. Unfortunately, the sad truth is that the government's record on children's rights is a far cry from the standards set out by the articles in the convention.
Article 18(2) requires a government to render appropriate child care services and facilities for the children of working parents. What has been the Tory response to this problem? After six years of promises, this government has failed to establish a long-awaited and much-needed national child care program.
Article 27 requires a government to "recognize the right of every child to a standard of living adequate for a child's physical, mental, spiritual, moral and social development".
As we see the rapidly increasing numbers of food bank users in this country, an estimated 40 per cent of them are children. Tens of thousands of Canadian children are dependent on food banks due to the Tory attack on universality, the clawback on family allowances, and the capping of the Canada Assistance Plan.
These are only two of many areas in which this Conservative government has failed Canada's children. Before the Prime Minister trots off to the world arena to lecture to world leaders on giving priority to children, he should make sure his own house is in order.

Mr. Speaker, it is autumn, young people are back in school, MPs are back in Parliament and Nova Scotia's Christmas tree growers are about to begin this year's harvest in earnest.
This weekend, the Lunenburg Christmas Tree Producers Association celebrate their 24th annual meeting and conference. We wish them well.
The Christmas tree industry yields some $70 million to Canadians and Lunenburg County, Canada's unquestioned Christmas tree capital, exports in excess of one million trees a year. These exports mean jobs for Canadians.
Soon the signs of Christmas will appear. I urge all Canadians and indeed all members to support Canada's Christmas tree industry this year by having a real Christmas tree.

Real Christmas trees are beautiful, environmentally friendly and one of Canada's great renewable resources.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I bring to the attention of the House the disruption of the ferry service between St. Barbe in the riding of my colleague from Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte and Blanc Sablon in the riding of Manicouagan as a result of a strike that has gone on all summer.
This ferry is the only link between the island of Newfoundland and southern Labrador. The disruption of the service at the height of the tourist season and in the midst of a fishery already in crisis has been devastating for both businesses and individuals.
This labour dispute must be resolved now and similar disruptions prevented in future in what I believe is an essential service. My colleague from Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte joins me in calling on the government to immediately bring labour and management to the table for a solution to the problem.
As well, the government should make special assistance available to those in tourism and the fishery who were crippled by the disruption of the service.
Finally, steps must be taken to deal with labour disputes in a manner that will not disrupt what, in effect, is a vital and essential service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister in the absence of the Prime Minister.
Oral Questions
Today, for the first time in our history, the Queen has created eight additional Senate seats, acting on the advice of the Prime Minister and his Cabinet.
Why did the Prime Minister give that advice to the Queen, rather than advising the Minister of Finance to withdraw the GST, the most unpopular tax in Canadian history, presented by the most unpopular government in Canadian history?
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Leader of the Opposition has been in this place for a long time and has been a very ardent student of parliamentary democracy. He knows very well that it is the obligation and, in fact, the duty of the duly elected Government of Canada to proceed with its legislative program and, indeed, to pass its legislative measures and particularly budgetary measures.
I think the hon. member recognizes that if the Senate were allowed to kill budgetary measures or block budgetary measures as it has and as it proposes to do so in the future, it would literally strangle the parliamentary process that we have and that we all respect and attempt to uphold. It is for that reason that these extraordinary actions had to be taken.
I simply remind the hon. member that the Senate has delayed three pieces of legislation currently before it, all of which have major financial implications: Bill C-21, the Unemployment Insurance bill which has been delayed for 10 months; Bill C-28, the large corporations tax which has been delayed for 9 months; and, Bill C-62 has been delayed for five months. We now have a motion before the Senate which states that the bill will not be proceeded with.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. leader's leader outside the House is on record as saying that he is going to kill the GST and there is no major financial bill that has ever been killed in the Senate before. That is why this unprecedented action is required.

Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the words of the Deputy Prime Minister sound rather hollow when he claims to be using undemocratic means to appoint unelected people to defend democracy. The words are hollow.
When our Constitution was repatriated in 1982, Canadians thought that they had a Constitution based in this country which would not be interpreted outside of Canada on the advice of the Prime Minister.
Right now a court in British Columbia is seized of the matter of the use of the clause in question of our Constitution. Why will the government not wait to appoint the eight additional senators until the British Columbia court has ruled on this matter? If this government is so concerned about the rule of law, why will it not refer the question itself to the Supreme Court of Canada today?
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the hon. Leader of the Opposition will want to re-read Article 26 of the Constitution of Canada which says:
If at any Time on the Recommendation of the Governor General the Queen thinks fit to direct that Four or Eight Members be added to the Senate, the Governor General may by Summons to Four or Eight qualified Persons (as the Case may be), representing equally the Four Divisions of Canada, add to the Senate accordingly.
That is pretty clear. It has been upheld in terms of our own legal advisors, plus a number of outside legal advisors who have shared that same view.
If we are going to uphold the fundamental principles of parliamentary democracy, we cannot allow an unelected body to run roughshod over the will of the people of Canada, namely as represented in the House of Commons.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):

method of the Constitution to ram through a measure opposed by 85 per cent of the Canadian people-

speechtext: -and when the government trying to thwart the will of 85 per cent of the Canadian people has the support of the lowest number since polling began in the country 50 years ago.
Hear! Hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):

speechtext:

What is the contingency plan of the federal government? If indeed these eight senators are deemed to be illegal senators, does that make the tax illegal? Are people going to be given refunds? What is the plan of the government if that indeed happens?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Housing.

as being very "corruptive", to paraphrase the words of the Deputy Prime Minister.

Oh, oh.

Your Honour then, quite properly, asked him to withdraw his remarks. He did withdraw, and Your Honour thanked him for it.

September 27, 1990
Point of Order
was intended to be accomplished, totally contrary to why we have these rules in place.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I take strong exception to those words.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, like all my colleagues, I heard what was said during Question Period. What we on this side of the House were criticizing today was the government's misuse of the Governor General's office for political and partisan ends. At no time did we ever question the role of the Queen or her prerogative to respond to a request from her Privy Council. What we did criticize was the Prime Minister's and the Conservative government's misuse of the Governor General's office.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order concerning an exchange with the Deputy Prime Minister earlier today in Question Period, in which he said, quite clearly, that Bill C-21 is being held up in the other place because of the opposition.
I think it is improper to misrepresent the progress of legislation through both our Houses. On May 10-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry. Many things are said on both sides of this House that are contradicted, corrected, adjusted or sometimes amended in the course of debate. We could go on all afternoon if we took those points
September 27, 1990

literally. The hon. member, clearly, has picked up something which he thinks is inaccurate and there are other ways to make that point.
I want to return for a moment, if we can finish up this matter which was raised by the hon. House leader. There are, of course, appropriate ways to take the rules which we have in front of the appropriate committee. If at any time hon. members wish to come into my office and discuss this, I would be only too pleased.
In the interest of the public that is watching us, let me point out the dilemma in which a Speaker finds himself or herself in a television age. Something may be said which is inappropriate but it is said. It is then on the electronic media. The Speaker of course, acting under centuries of tradition and according to the rules, asks an hon. member to withdraw or to put the matter in a more appropriate way. Several examples of that were found today and I have to say on both sides of the House there were withdrawals.
What is almost impossible for a Speaker to do, though, is to stop the comment before it is made. Sometimes, because I have an incredible ability to define what is coming, I am able to cut off a speaker before the speaker has spoken. But it does not happen very often and usually it leads to a member visiting my office saying: "What was it you thought I was going to say?" If I tell him or her I may be insulting them, and other times I may have given them a marvellous thought. In any event, you see the difficulty.
On a more serious note-fortunately, we did not have this today-some time ago I had to remark that comments made in preambles, while clearly out of line, after they are said can do great damage to people across the country. To a remarkable degree, and I thank all hon. members for this, there has been a lot of co-operation in keeping that in mind.
Today some things were said which I felt ought not to have been said and they have been withdrawn. I have to point out to all hon. members that ultimately this place depends on the self-discipline of everybody because the Speaker can correct, the Speaker can force a withdrawal, the Speaker can even dismiss a member. It does not stop the fact that things are said. Things are on the electronic
Business of the House
media and of course once there, they are no longer the property of this place.
I would ask all hon. members, especially when we are in matters of great importance, to keep those things in mind. I know all hon. members will try to co-operate.
I think we need the usual business question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether it is the duty or responsibility of the Opposition House Leader to ask for the minutes but he has been doing it. Certainly I want to co-operate with him and provide as much forewarning as possible.
Today, we will continue with the Iraq motion. I hope the discussions can carry on across the floor and other ways so that we could find a way to reach a conclusion on that debate at some time. If there is a desire to extend hours to allow more people to speak, we would be co-operative with that. We want to give everybody in the House who wants to participate an opportunity to participate in the debate, but at some point in time we would like to bring it to a conclusion as well and have it voted on.
Tomorrow, I would hope to continue with the report stage of Bill C-44; perhaps also to complete second reading of Bill C-73, a technical and administrative bill dealing with the Crown Corporation Dissolution Act. There is a time question involved and it would be helpful to the smooth administration of the dissolution of these

September 27, 1990
Business of the House
obsolete Crown corporations if we could have that passed. I hope I could receive the co-operation of the opposition in that regard.
On Monday, the agenda to some extent will depend on the progress we make today and tomorrow. In all likelihood I will be calling Bill C-44, the Hibernia energy legislation, hopefully for completion. In the meantime, we will carry on our usual discussions respecting further business.
In terms of whether or not there is going to be a by-election in Beausejour, one thing I can say with great certainty is that the Prime Minister would relish the opportunity of getting the new "la petite garde du Nouveau Brunswick" in the House and will not present an obstacle.

Mr. Speaker, I want to raise a question with the House Leader.
As he knows, at the beginning of the week I submitted a motion for an emergency debate on the question of the World Summit for Children. I also raised the question directly with the Prime Minister who responded in the House-I believe it was on Tuesday-in a positive way, saying he thought it would be an important opportunity for members of Parliament to express the concerns of their constituents.
There was an indication that there might be a day called before the Prime Minister left for New York. I gather from what the House Leader just said that it is not possible.
In that circumstance, I wonder if the House Leader would be prepared to designate a day next week after the return of the Prime Minister when we have at least seen what the statements were. Members of Parliament would have the opportunity to present what is a very strong and compelling concern of many of our constituents about children's rights and how that is being approached in the international area. It would be certainly in accordance with the Prime Minister's wishes, because he so expressed himself in the House on Tuesday.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, indeed, he did and we did make some efforts to see if that could be accomplished. Having the situation with the Iraq motion, which I am sure the hon. member agreed we needed to proceed with in the House, we had tried to get extended hours on Monday but failed to get consent of the opposition in that regard. Of course, we needed to proceed with the Oka motion, as well as having other legislative business.
We did talk some about perhaps using an allotted opposition day for that purpose but, quite rightfully, the hon. member's House leader said the opposition will decide the subject of opposition days and I will not try to interfere.
On the general question, we would like to be accommodating in achieving a debate on that very important subject. The only caveat I put to that is that we do have some very important legislation and other items on which I need to receive progress. If we can have our usual discussions and achieve agreement on that, we will certainly be ready and more than willing to co-operate.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with care to the response of the House Leader and I recognize the difficulties sometimes in arranging House business. I would make the case that I do not think that there is anything more important right now than the concern about children.
While we have a veiy full agenda, as he well knows, we are just back in the first week. We have a nice long time ahead of us through to December and these issues will continue to be debated. I hope that in the next week the government will designate its own day and resolution.
The Prime Minister has taken a role as the co-chair of the summit and it has been a matter of very intense discussion across the country. It would be a very important opportunity for Canadians, not only to hear from the Prime Minister on his return from the United Nations, but for us to reciprocate with our views on behalf of so many Canadians.
I really would urge the House Leader and I am sure he will find full co-operation from this side.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let there be no mistake in terms of the priority. The mere fact that the Prime Minister of Canada is chairing this international confer-
September 27, 1990

ence on children is an indication of the importance that the government places on it.
What I do have to ask, perhaps a bit with tongue in cheek, whether debates in the House are very healthy for children, especially their mental health, given what happened earlier here today.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps if we had a designated day for debate on the rights of children, we might show them that this Parliament, maybe once in a while, will live up to their expectation. We expect the House Leader to show some leadership in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that I have to raise a matter that arose in Question Period yesterday. I have drawn the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact that I was to raise this matter.
In Hansard at page 13447, he made reference to me and, based on a newspaper article which I understand appeared in The Ottawa Citizen on September 19, he alleged that I stated things that I simply did not state. Knowing him to be an honourable man, I am sure that he has had time now to see that he misspoke himself in saying that I advanced this position and I would hope that, in the circumstances, he would be prepared to withdraw and apologize.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I think my friend opposite is getting just a little tender.
The quote that he was referring to, if I can read it back to him, is this: "Our credibility"-this is the Liberal Party's credibility-"will be in shreds if we don't come up with a thoughtful alternative to tax reform that stands up to scrutiny."
The point that I was making yesterday is that here we have the Liberal Party in the other place, the unelected senators, saying: "We are going to kill this bill." We saw in the House today where it is fully supported by the
Government Orders
other members of the Liberal Party here and, at the same time, by implication, the member from Ottawa is saying: "We have no alternative to this bill."
The point that I was making to the member for Acadie-Bathurst is that it is quite incredible to me that the Liberal Party would be killing a bill which the business community has said will throw the business sector into chaos over a period of time if not dealt with. At the same time, the member is saying clearly, by implication, that there is no alternative, that they have not come up with any alternative. Since 1987 we have had a white paper on sales tax reform and an election campaign when the party said that it was not going to go ahead with sales tax reform and it really astounds me that this party has not come up with an alternative.
I say to my hon. friends that if they do have an alternative they should say so. But if they do not have an alternative, they should recognize that their credibility is in shreds, recognize that they have no legitimacy in raising these questions in the House, recognize that the Senate has no legitimacy in-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member for Ottawa South would want to respond.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that my presumption concerning the minister appears to have been wrong. He correctly read from the article. I said and am quoted as saying: "Our credibility will be in shreds if we don't come up with a thoughtful alternative to tax reform that stands up to scrutiny." In fact, his tax is what is going to create chaos and the alternative to it is to put it in the shredding

September 27, 1990
Government Orders
machines in his office and forget it, before he drives the country crazy.

Mr. Speaker, my word was not "chaos". They have not stated what their alternative is. In fact, they very proudly say-
Point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you indicated, prior to Question Period I had expressed my concern and my support for the motion before the House with respect to the fact that the House condemn the unprovoked invasion of Kuwait by Iraq and also the support for Canada's actions at the United Nations, as well as for the support for the dispatch of Canadian forces to the Arabian Peninsula.

I had indicated that with all the black clouds and the frightening aspects of this entire situation, there are some bright spots. The brightest spot, as I indicated, in my view at least, is the role that the United Nations is playing in the development process that is going on in the United Nations, an evolutionary process which I compared to the evolution of the British parliamentary system, which has taken many many hundreds of years and is still going on.
Hopefully, we are now in the process of evolving that institution of the United Nations into something that will be much more effective as a governing body in the world, much more effective in policing against unprovoked aggression and much more effective in dealing with the kinds of problems we have had and will continue to have in the world, much more effective than it has been heretofore, when it certainly has been a most ineffective body as far as Canadians in general are concerned, and people around the world.
I had started to examine some of the concerns that have been expressed by Canadians and by members of this House with respect to the various actions that have been taken by the government and the motion itself.
One of those concerns relates to the question of United Nations authorization for the action of Canadian forces and other forces in the Persian Gulf and the Arabian Peninsula area. That is an understandable concern in my view.
In light of my comments previously that at the same time this evolving role of the United Nations is understandable, we certainly have not come to the point where the institution of the United Nations can react as quickly as we would like it to. Perhaps in the past it has not been able to react at all except in very limited cases, and well after the fact.
I think what we see here is a circumstance of unprovoked aggression on the part of Iraq. The threat that Iraqi forces would roll on into Saudi Arabia and roll on into other parts of the Middle East provides a need for an immediate response on the part of other United Nations countries in order to counteract that just as quickly as they possibly could. To seek authorization after the fact is exactly what has happened in this case.
Government Orders
We trust that in this ongoing process in dealing with this situation, we will be able to obtain United Nations approval and mandate before any other actions are taken. Obviously, there are circumstances in which Canadian or other forces might have to react before there is such a mandate. There might have to be an effort to try to obtain that mandate after the fact.
I think the significant part here is that we should not be allowing one nation, or a group of nations, to proceed without attempting to get that United Nations mandate.
In fact, as you are aware-unfortunately, I do not believe too many Canadians are aware-Canada has played a leading role at the United Nations in trying to get authority and a mandate for all the actions that have taken place. Although I have not seen too many reports in the Canadian press about this, there are reports in The New York Times.
I would just like to briefly refer to an article in The New York Times of August 14 of this year which indicated that Canada had, and I quote:
- indicated today that a new resolution authorizing the use of force under Article 42 of the Charter would be required before countries could legally use warships to enforce the sanctions.
In fact, Canada has been playing a leading role at the United Nations and in all other discussions on a bilateral and multilateral basis in order to ensure that there is a United Nations mandate and that one nation, whether it be the United States or any other nation, is not acting on its own, but there is a concerted effort as we have seen and it does have United Nations sanction.
Again, I hope that we can develop a process whereby this will be more automatic. This will work faster and certainly more easily in the days ahead in other crises of this sort, hopefully less severe than this sort.
Another concern that has been expressed to me by some of my constituents-not all but certainly some of them and certainly by members of this House who have pointed out their concern-that we would be sending Canadian forces to the Arabian Peninsula, to the Persian Gulf before Parliament had actually had an opportunity to sit, debate and discuss the matter.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the provisions of the National Defence Act, the provisions of Canadian convention and tradition in this case have been followed.

September 27, 1990
Government Orders
They have been followed exactly in accordance with those traditions.
It is understandable, however, that Canadians should feel that this was an important matter, that Parliament should be called and have the opportunity to debate the matter even though the National Defence Act provides that there is no obligation for Parliament ever to vote on this issue in any way whatsoever, but only to be called to sit in a situation of this sort.
What disturbed me more than anything else was, when some Canadians were expressing this concern and members of Parliament were expressing this concern, when the matter was placed before the House on Monday, the very first day, there was an opportunity for the debate to be continued, perhaps for the entire evening and into the night and, perhaps it could have gone on for several days. Unfortunately, the opposition members of this House refused to give their consent to carry on that debate, notwithstanding the fact that they and other Canadians were expressing concern that this was such an important issue and that it should be brought before the House and debate fully as quickly as possible. I, for one, am dismayed that we were not able to carry on in that fashion with the continuing debate.
Another concern that has been expressed-

speechtext: The hon. member for Burnaby-Kings-way on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I do hesitate to interrupt the hon. member but I know that he would want the record to be set straight. When he suggested that opposition members on Monday were not prepared to continue the debate, I know he would want the record to show that, in fact, the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party were both fully prepared to continue that debate, however, it was an Independent member of the House who apparently was not prepared at that time to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate the hon. member's intervention. Whoever it was that was not prepared to continue the debate, it was someone in the opposition benches of the House.
Another aspect that Canadians and members of the House have expressed concern about has to do with the
fact that there is no United Nations flag flying over the forces in the Persian Gulf. The forces are not wearing blue berets and there is no specifically designated United Nations commander. I, for one, hope that all of those things will happen and happen as quickly as possible.
Mr. Speaker, you recall and I recall and I am sure other members of this House are too young to recall the Korean war. We recall that those things did not happen immediately in the Korean war either. They took a little bit of time to get into place and, hopefully, we can get them back into place more quickly than occurred in the Korean war. Hopefully, we will be able to put in place a mechanism so that those things happen more automatically in the days ahead but this is an evolving process and I think all of us should bear that in mind.
Another concern that has been expressed, particularly by some of my constituents who are Canadians of the Muslim faith, is a concern about the whole situation as it relates to the Middle Eastern situation and their roles. Some of these constituents of mine have their origin in the Middle East from a variety of Arab states and there is, just as there is in the Middle East itself, some differences of opinion within those Arab states. Those same differences of opinion are expressed here in Canada as well. I think it is important for all of us to recognize that these are Canadians who originate from countries in that part of the world, Canadians who have legitimate concerns about their families and friends, their origins and their roots which are not always the same perspective that many other Canadians may have. It is important to bear those in mind because we are talking about the concerns of Canadians.
I have suggested to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that what we need is a consultative group, perhaps something like we had in relation to the difficulties a short time ago in China. In that case we had a consultative group of Canadians of Chinese origin who were able to express the concerns of Canadians to the government and to the Secretary of State. They were able to hear the reasoning, the rationale and the position of the government and were able to act as a two-way line of communication between Canadians of Chinese origin, in that case, and the government and Canadians generally-

I think it is important thing that we should be establishing here too with respect to Canadians of Arab origin, Canadians of Muslim origin and the government in a situation like this when there are substantial differences of opinion, concerns, concepts, ideas, and information which have to be communicated back and forth so that everybody fully understands what is going on and why it is going on.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has indicated to me that he is favourably inclined toward that sort of thing. I would like to take this occasion to urge him to proceed as quickly as possible with the creation of such an organization. I can tell him that among Canadians of the Muslim faith now a nation-wide organization has been created and is still in the evolving state which would fit in perfectly with that idea. I truly believe that it would be extremely valuable in this situation to have such a consultative body.
Mr. Speaker, you have indicated that my time is up. I would just like to close by indicating once again that I believe we are in an evolving state as far as the United Nations is concerned. In my view this is a tremendous step toward being able to deal with aggression in a collective form, in a form of collective security with an international mandate. It is even more important and is setting a significant precedent. Every time we do something like this, it is very difficult the next time to do something different. Having taken a collective international approach to this under the United Nations, it is going to be harder the next time we are faced with a crisis like this not to do the same.
I commend that to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and to you, Mr. Speaker. This is something that will be helpful to all Canadians and to everyone around the world.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with my colleague and I thank him and the NDP for putting on the record that it certainly was not any member of the Official Opposition in this House who objected to extended hours on this debate on Monday evening.
However, I find it surprising that my colleague across the floor appears to be defending his government which in my opinion acted against both precedent and principle in the way it has handled the Middle East crisis;
Government Orders
precedent in terms of not recalling Parliament when this nation was faced with one of the greatest crisis of the last decade, and the principle of this country in always trying to follow UN precedent when becoming involved in any international action.
Is my colleague across the floor suggesting that it was acceptable that this House was not reconvened and that the government sent Canadian Armed Forces into the arena two weeks before a UN resolution to support such action was brought forth and gained approval?

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately I gather that the hon. member was not listening to my remarks because I addressed both of the issues that she has referred to. I certainly welcome the opportunity to reiterate the positions that I put.
As I indicated quite clearly, as far as the recall of Parliament is concerned, the provisions of the National Defence Act and the provisions of Canadian convention and practice with respect to the recalling of Parliament in a situation of this sort have been followed and in fact at the earliest possible opportunity when the House met on Monday. As the hon. member is aware, there was the opportunity right off the bat to discuss and debate all aspects of this issue.
The Canadian Forces are still not fully in place in accordance with the expectations of where they will be. Hon. members of the opposition have the opportunity to express a feeling that perhaps they should be recalled and brought back to Canada, if that is what the hon. member is saying. Perhaps I have missed it, but I have not heard any member of the House, to the best of my knowledge, indicate that he or she feels that we should be recalling our forces.
I suspect the great concern here is about the opportunity for the House to be called and to have a debate. Of course that is what we are having now and it will continue, I take it, as long as Your Honour feels it is appropriate. The debate can go on and on and on. The hon. member and other members of the opposition, as will other members of the government, will have the opportunity to express themselves.
If the hon. member truly feels that the Canadian forces should be recalled and should not be there, I think it is important that she and other members of the House

Government Orders
who have similar feelings should stand up and tell us so that that will be clear.
On the other issue that the hon. member raised, again I thought that I had addressed that fully in my comments. I believe I did, but I do not mind trying again to explain it, perhaps in a different way, or adding a few more facts or whatever.
In that case the hon. member asked a question relating to the United Nations authorization and acting before there was full and complete authorization by the United Nations.
Again I repeat the fact that all these circumstances took place in the context of very rapid, unexpected, unprovoked aggression by Iraq into Kuwait, and with the prospect of rolling on into Saudi Arabia and perhaps rolling on into other middle eastern countries as well. In light of that it was necessary, in my view, for other United Nations governments to take some action there in order to head that off at the pass.
It would have been very nice if we had had a process in place at the United Nations where all we had to do was call one meeting, and snap: everything would role into place. We would have a United Nations peacekeeping force that was already organized and could be called upon at the drop of a hat to move into place to deal with those sorts of things.
Unfortunately the United Nations, which was founded at the end of the Second World War as the hon. member is aware, has been a world institution for which we have all had great hopes. We have all had great faith in it, but it has not frankly been very effective in dealing with issues of this sort. One of the reasons why is that there has been a great power struggle between East and West in this world, which only now seems to be coming to some sort of an end.
Now we have had for the first time both the United States and the USSR acting together in a common front in dealing with a problem of this sort. It is an evolving process. It is one that I think we should all applaud. Hopefully we will be able to bring it to a stage where the United Nations can react very quickly, but in the meantime surely we should be acting and then getting the approval as quickly as we can after the fact.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. member a question
with respect to the point he made concerning the current siting of the three Canadian vessels. Originally it was the intention of the Canadian Armed Forces to locate these vessels in the Gulf of Oman, as the hon minister is no doubt aware. At some point that decision was changed and it was decided to send the three vessels into the heart of the possible conflict zone, through the Straits of Hormuz and into the Persian Gulf.
I want to ask the minister whether he agrees with the suggestion that I have made and that I understand is supported by the Official Opposition as well, that in fact the ships we have sent should not be brought back to Canada as the member indicated but should pull back to the Gulf of Oman where they would be in a position to enforce resolution 665, the resolution that results in the enforcement of sanctions which were imposed under 661. At the same time they would not be at risk in the event of a possible offensive military strike by the United States.
At this point there is no United Nations command. There is always a risk that that kind of first strike might in fact take place by the United States and that the men and women from CF-18 squadron and the ships could have their lives put at risk.
Is the minister prepared to recommend to his colleagues in cabinet that our ships pull back to the Gulf of Oman? They perform an important role in terms of enforcement of the United Nations resolution, but the lives of Canadian men and women must not be put at risk by the possibility of a unilateral American strike not under the auspices of the United Nations?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. minister has a couple of minutes to answer that question.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has expressed concern about the command structure of the United Nations forces in the gulf area. That in itself should lead the hon. member to conclude that there has to be some co-operation, some discussion, and some interaction among all of the forces there, Canadian and other forces. Obviously that is what has been going on and why there may be changes. There may be further changes in the way in which our forces are located or stationed in that area.
If the hon. member is suggesting that we station our forces in one particular place-I am not sure whether or not that is in his motion-that will be most interesting. I
September 27, 1990

do not claim to be a military expert or one who knows anything about the formalities of strategy or tactics, but common sense leads me to believe that when one is in an area in which there could be some sort of conflict or some sort of action, there has to be a good deal of flexibility. That has to be left to the military commanders to be able to make judgments and make decisions not restricted surely by politicians. I think they tried in ancient Rome to have politicians run armies, but I do not think they were too successful.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wanted to make it clear that this member has misinterpreted words and put words into my mouth. I have not in this House or anywhere for one instance suggested that our Canadian Armed Forces should be withdrawn from the region. I just wanted to make that clear for the record.

Mr. Speaker, barely a month ago more than 900 young men and women sailed out of Halifax harbour on three ships. This is not an event that is unusual in the history of Halifax.
The city of Halifax is over 241 years old. It was founded as a garrison town. It has been a naval base for all those 240 years. It is known, at least in literary circles, as the warden of the north. It is the closest port to Europe. Its citizens are well aware of the responsibilities and the meaning of the word war.
In World War II ships were sunk off the mouth of Halifax Harbour. Indeed, one Christmas early in the war the corvette Clayoquoit went down within sight of shore and within sight of many Haligonians. During that war as well the population of Halifax doubled with the numbers of servicemen and their families moving into the city which was known in many parts of North America as the only city on the continent that really was at war.
Government Orders
Haligonians became very familiar with the sight of merchant men and navy ships limping back into harbour suffering the ravages of war in the North Atlantic. They became very familiar with waving good-bye to young men who went down to the sea in ships and never returned. They understand what it means and they understand what the defence of freedom is all about. Halagonians, as well as all Canadians, have always been prepared to make the sacrifices necessary to defend freedom and to stop aggression at home or abroad. In Halifax we are proud of our services. We are proud of our navy, in particular. Our navy is small but for over 75 years it has sailed with pride, eliciting admiration from allies and grudging admiration from enemies.
Mr. Speaker, we are also proud of our shipyard workers who were called on at the beginning of the gulf crisis and who readied the three ships in less than two weeks. Again, when Halagonians are called on they answer and they come forward.
The last war-and I used that term in quotation marks-Canadians were exposed to on a personal basis was that which was known as the police action in Korea. But since the early 1950s Canada's Armed Forces have been the premier peacekeepers of our global village. Canadians accept that role with pride and, indeed, it is the role that they have come to expect from their armed forces. Make no mistake, Canadians, Halagonians in particular, were appalled by the actions of Saddam Hussein and were prepared to play their role in maintaining peace and security, both in the Middle East and world-wide. Again I reiterate, never have Canadians been called and found wanting in situations of this nature.
That last very sunny Friday in August, I stood on a Halifax pier with some of my colleagues from this House with feelings of pride and trepidation. These feelings, I know, were shared by the vast majority of my constituents. I am sure that they were shared to a degree by the vast majority of Canadians. But I think I have to use perhaps a little special pleading in this case, that because of the things I have said, because of our unique geography, because Halifax is the largest naval base in the country, there is perhaps in the citizens of Halifax and Dartmouth a bit more awareness, a bit more experience in areas of this nature. This is not to denigrate other

Government Orders
Canadians who feel very strongly. It is just a fact of life and it is very much a fact of life in Halifax-Dartmouth.
I watched Protecteur, Terra Nova and Athabaskan as they sailed out of Halifax harbour. I wished for three things. First and foremost, that these young men and women would return safely to our port, unharmed and unscarred by any battle. Second, I wished that this operation was securely under United Nations auspices. Third, I wished that the duly elected representatives of the people of this country from all parties had been given the chance to make their views known before the ships were sent.
Mr. Speaker, I was out of the country shortly after the crisis arose in the Middle East. I noticed, watching both CNN, the American news network, and I believe it is called Skyline, the European news network. I noticed
Skyway.

-Skyway, whatever; at any rate, the European English news network. I noticed that every single night representatives of our allies were on television talking to their citizenry about what was happening. George Bush, whether it was from the golf course or fishing boat, was speaking to the American people every night. Margaret Thatcher, from various locations was speaking to her people every night.
Mr. Speaker, Great Britain's Parliament was recalled. VAssemblee nationale de France was recalled. President Bush consulted widely with members of Congress and with members of the Senate of both political parties in the United States. Again, the people in these countries were constantly made aware by their leaders of what was going on, of what was developing. At least the sight of their leaders on their nation's television networks gave some form of reassurance.
Sadly, no such developments took place in Canada. Our government acted without the broad consultation that Canadians expected. Our Prime Minister did not come before the Canadian people to inform and reassure them. Indeed, on that sunny day when the ships sailed out of our historic port, he did not even come to Halifax to show his support for our forces going east. It was noticed and his absence will be long remembered.
The families of our forces in Halifax are uneasy. It is not that they are unwilling to sacrifice. It is not that they
do not know what it means when their sons and daughters, husbands and wives, mothers and fathers enlist in our armed forces. They know what it means, but they are uneasy.
The question of who is in charge has never been fully resolved. It has never been fully answered to the satisfaction of my constituents in the city of Halifax.
The citizens of Halifax are always prepared to defend freedom and preserve the peace. But they and all Canadians deserve to be informed. They deserve to be informed of policy and they deserve to be represented in the decision-making process.
It really is not fair. The stress of having a family member in a war zone is enough. It should not have been exacerbated by a government that hid from its people.
In war and peace Canadians have always shouldered the burden of duty and performed gloriously. But since the days of Lester B. Pearson, the man whom we all delighted to honour here yesterday, our emphasis has been UN related and peace oriented. Indeed, our peacekeepers shared in the Nobel Prize just a few short years ago. I might add that Nobel Prize was in the grand tradition of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson.
Earlier today the hon. parliamentary secretary referred to Canadian blood spilled in the past. I know full well that he agrees with me that we all wish to avoid bloody conflict, but that Canadians have never shirked when their duty was clear.
The tragedy here is that we are veering from our long-established process. The government by veering from our long-established process has created a form of uncertainty and unease among the populous. Part of that uncertainty and unease arises from the fact that Canadians, who have always done their duty, are almost afraid to come out and say that unease is there. They are almost afraid because they do not want to be thought to be unsupportive of our people who are going to the Persian Gulf. I do not think there is anyone in this House who does not support our personnel in the Persian Gulf, but equally I think that the majority of Canadians need to be reassured that we are under UN auspices. We need to have the UN in charge of this operation and we need to see that Canadians are acting in the interests of peace and stability.
September 27, 1990

My party condemns outright the doings of Iraq and Saddam Hussein in his invasion of Kuwait. We condemn Hussein's use of Canadians and other foreign nationals as human shields. We condemn him and all his works and pomps, but we remind this government, as it so desperately needs to be reminded, that Canada is an independent country with long-standing ties to the United Nations and its processes. Canada is not a colonial choreboy for the United States. We are not here to save the American oil patch.
The recall of Parliament in the summer of 1987 is something even those of us who were not so fortunate as to be in the Chamber at the time remember well. Again, it is something the Haligonians and Nova Scotians remember very well. I believe it was 157 cold, tired, and wet Tamils who were literally thrown off a freighter in Clark's Harbour, Shelburne County, Nova Scotia. They straggled ashore, to be met-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext: Sikhs in Nova Scotia, Tamils in Newfoundland.

Sorry. Neither the number nor the nationality is important. I think my friends in the government and my friends in the NDP both get the point. The point is that these poor refugees straggled ashore in Clark's Harbour and the denizens of Shelburne County went down and fed them peanut butter sandwiches on the beach-they did not know where these people came from as, clearly, the member from Halifax was not too sure either-so that they did not infringe on any of their dietary laws. That is why they brought them peanut butter sandwiches.
But because of these harmless people on our shores in Nova Scotia, we had to recall Parliament. However, we did not recall Parliament when we sent nearly 1,000 young people to a war zone. It goes beyond belief. If the people of Clark's Harbour, Shelburne County, Nova Scotia, were not afraid of the refugees, I find it unusual that Parliament had to act, especially in light of the fact, and I understand and I am sure that my learned colleagues will correct me, that it took well over a year to get the bill for which Parliament was recalled passed. There seems to be an emphasis in the wrong direction somewhere.
It is sad that we did not use our considerable influence in the United Nations to ensure that this was an UN-directed operation before our people went. Instead,
Government Orders
with its usual desire to follow the United States, the government bypassed our traditions and, most important, the government bypassed our premier, democratic institution, the House of Commons. There has been a lot of talk about democracy in the last few days. The word has been bandied about in a manner that a lot of us find disagreeable.
To send young Canadians into a war zone without the debate and the approval of Parliament I think is an attack on democracy of the first order. Our forces will do the job they are asked to do and they will do it well. And never for one instance should their families and their friends be allowed to think that they do not have our full support and our proud admiration, that is a given. But it is sad, no it goes beyond sad, it is tragic that in hurrying off to defend freedom, in hurrying off to ensure that Canada was following the dictates of the United States, in haring off not, I suspect most sadly, because of the threats but more because of the request of our neighbour to the south, we have seen our own democratic traditions and our own duly-elected democratic representatives in Parliament bypassed and denigrated by the Canadian government.
I started out by talking about the city of Halifax because, of course, for the people of Halifax and Dartmouth this is more than just a national issue, it is a very personal story. On that Friday afternoon when I and some of my colleagues from this House and other people stood on the wharf, we watched the ships go and we watched three old ships. We know that those old ships with their young personnel will do the job. But we never ever stop worrying. We never ever stop praying that the Government of Canada will see the light, return to our traditions, and use its considerable influence before the United Nations now, even after the fact, to ensure that this operation is United Nations driven and United Nations sponsored.
This is what Canadians deserve and expect. It is what those young men and women in the gulf deserve and expect. It is the very least that parliamentarians such as ourselves should demand.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to get back to the role of the United Nations. First, however, I would like to say that I was listening carefully to the hon. member's speech and I had expected her to

Government Orders
comment on the absence of the Prime Minister. I fully expected her to do that.
She mentioned earlier that the Prime Minister did not speak to the nation. I think he made it quite clear at various press conferences what the reasons were and what principles were at stake. He was always ready to explain. But since you mentioned that the Prime Minister was not around, I would like to ask where her leader was. Her leader was in Italy on vacation and he did not come rushing back. Why didn't you mention that both ministers of National Defence were there? No, you wanted to show the Prime Minister was not around. Do you know where he was?
I also wanted to talk about the United Nations.
We want to know where he was.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Just call 992-4211 and you will find out. Find out, instead of accusing people! And I suggest you ask where Chretien was. He was away on holiday in Italy.
As for the United Nations, Mr. Speaker, I would like to repeat here in the House a fact that mentioned several times in the media, especially in the American press. Of course, when a Canadian does something right, he doesn't get much coverage in the Canadian press. However, Ambassador Fortier in New York has been absolutely extraordinary. He did his job. He fulfilled his mission. Canada is a member of the Security Council and, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member would do well to stress the leadership role we played in this area by achieving a consensus in what must have been record time at the United Nations, when we realize that customarily, it takes a long time to reach a consensus at that level. Our action was successful. And if you read the Washington Post or the New York Times, you will realize how much the work done by Ambassador Fortier, Canada's ambassador to the United Nations, was appreciated.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity to answer my hon. colleague from Beauhar-nois-Salaberry.
Perhaps he is suggesting that I should make phone calls to find out the answers to questions, some phone calls it is not necessary for me to make. I know for a fact that Mr. Chretien was not invited to the farewell on the
wharf, and I know for an equal fact that the Right Hon. Prime Minister was invited.
As to where my leader was at the time, my leader was well represented by the hon. member for Halifax and the hon. member for Dartmouth.
I certainly stated that there were other colleagues in the House. If the hon. member wishes me to put it on the record, the Minister of National Defence was there and the Associate Minister of National Defence was there. But the Prime Minister was not there. The Prime Minister called one press conference. It was very short and he answered very few questions.
I referred to President Bush and Mrs. Thatcher. Neither political leader, I might add, do I often refer to in an admiring manner, either in the House or anywhere else. But, as leaders of their countries, my hon. friend should know, they came on television every night during the early days of this crisis and informed their people. Where was our Prime Minister, the leader of this country? Where was he? If you know, fine. I did not know and I doubt that many Canadians knew. I also doubt that a phone call would have told us, because there were many of families in Halifax-Dartmouth who gladly would have expended the quarter to find out where the Prime Minister was.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Halifax on an excellent speech. I certainly share the concerns that she raised during her speech regarding her many constituents from Halifax. Her colleague from Dartmouth also spoke very eloquently during the debate on Monday from that perspective as well, as a representative of a riding with many men and women who are families of those who have gone into this very, very difficult mission. We pay tribute to those who have undertaken this measure.
Does the hon. member for Halifax agree with the suggestion that I have made and that others have made that the original tasking of these ships should be maintained? That is, the original destination which was the Gulf of Oman, outside the possible range of Iraqi missiles, would have been a more appropriate place for these ships to perform their functions because they would, as well, be under the auspices of Resolution 665 of the United Nations, instead of going through the Straits of Hormuz into the zone of conflict or directly into the Persian Gulf. Does she agree that they should be sited in the Gulf of Oman at least until such time as the forces in that region come under a unified United

Nations command? We are speaking here of all forces, including the American forces, under a United Nations command and the hon. member has spoken very eloquently of the need for that. To avoid the risk to the men and women on those ships and in that CF-18 squadron, does she agree that it would be far more appropriate to site them in the Gulf of Oman?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague from Burnaby-Kingsway. Perhaps, if I may be allowed to instruct un peu, they are still under Resolution 665 even though they have gone into the Straits of Hormuz. They are in a more dangerous position but they are still covered at this point by Resolution 665. That is not strictly the answer to the question, I realize, but I have no qualms as long as they are under the UN resolution. I have no qualms in the procedural sense, if you will, other than the qualms I clearly stated before.
Second, clearly, as the member for Halifax and as the representative for those families, those children and those parents, I do not want any of my constituents or their families in the range of Iraqi missiles. But I guess you have to do what you sign up to do.

Mr. Speaker, I have a very brief supplementary question.
The member will know that in fact our troops in the region have two tasks. One is under United Nations Resolution 665, but the other is as part of the American-led mandate to deter possible aggression. Of course, it is that second element of the mandate which places our troops at risk. The possibility of a unilateral offensive, a possible American-led offensive, would place our troops at far greater risk if they are in the heart of the Persian Gulf under that part of the mandate than if they were in the Gulf of Oman. I trust that the hon. member recognizes that even though they would be under Resolution 665 wherever they are enforcing the sanctions, it is that second element of their mandate which poses the risk.

Mr. Speaker, I think that the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway and I are in agreement on what is actually taking place, in the sense of what comes behind the theories, sadly, of both our government and the American government. However, while they are
Government Orders
under 665, both the opposition parties have called for UN auspices. Resolution 665 is the UN auspices. The second part of the mandate, if you will, is unfortunately still something we can only surmise. Our surmise may be indeed extremely logical, accurate, and true but it is still something we can only surmise. While 665 holds, I do not have a problem with 665.

I do not know the exact disposition, but I know the American forces are there. They have mutual support and they have air cover. So, while they are within the range of the Exocet missile and the Mirage aircraft, which is perhaps the biggest threat to our ships, in fact they can be under the same threat if these Mirages refuel which they can do. In effect, while they may be under a greater threat, it is my assessment in my present position, and not being on the scene at the time, that perhaps they have better mutual support. They may be as well off, or perhaps even better off, in the Persian Gulf.
The point is that it is very dangerous for us, as politicians, to debate where military forces should be stationed as much as we would like to do. This surely is the prerogative of the Chief of the Defence Staff and the

military commander at the scene, Commodore Summers.
