speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to address the House today on a matter of public concern, a matter of both national and international importance. My purpose in speaking today is principally twofold. First, I would like to explain to the House the significance of the events in the Persian Gulf as they relate to Canada's energy situation and, second, I would like to explain the actions that the Government of Canada is taking to respond to those events.
Members of the House, as this debate also indicates, have followed with great interest the impact of Iraq's invasion of Kuwait and the subsequent events that have followed in international oil markets. I want to assure the House and all Canadians that the government remains well informed on the rapidly changing events in the gulf. The situation in the Middle East is both volatile and highly unpredictable. It is true that crude oil prices have risen and remain unstable, but that is to be expected in a situation where the markets remain jittery and the price of a barrel of oil has almost doubled in the last two months.
Despite these uncertainties, our refiners are currently having no difficulty obtaining crude oil supplies. The result of the present embargo of oil shipments from Iraq and Kuwait is the loss to the international oil market of approximately 4.1 million barrels per day. Fortunately, in response to this, there have been some production increases from other OPEC and non-OPEC countries, particularly from Saudi Arabia and Venezuela. This additional production is now reaching significant levels and part of the shortfall in world production is also being made up by drawing down commercial stocks and from somewhat lower oil product demand. This combination of higher production in non-affected areas, stock draw,
and demand reduction should be sufficient to avoid a serious tightening of the world oil market for some time. The situation remains manageable.
But there are, as I think members of the House have indicated in this debate, many uncertainties inherent in the present situation. The oil market is likely to become increasingly tighter during the winter months when oil demand is seasonally highest and as the capacity for significant additional supplies gradually diminishes. The situation could also be affected by any unexpected occurrences such as a colder than normal winter or problems with transportation and refining facilities. Over the next several months oil prices are likely to remain volatile as markets respond to a number of factors, including underlying supply-demand pressures, rumours and short-term competitive pressures. So, obviously, the situation bears close watching.
Notwithstanding the inability of governments, industry and the International Energy Agency, the IEA, to precisely quantify the magnitude of any possible future oil supply problem, there is consensus that the global oil markets will tighten and Canadian markets will be similarly affected.
The recent increases in motor gasoline prices in Canada, for example, are evidence that our country cannot be insulated from world oil uncertainties. Canada's response to the Persian Gulf situation has been within the framework of our existing policies on security of supply and emergency preparedness.
The point of departure for present Canadian policy is that energy markets must be allowed to respond effectively and efficiently to changes in supply-demand conditions, both internationally and in the domestic market. Canada's economy is part of that world market.
Efforts of previous governments to insulate us from world energy economy through regulation of prices and trade simply did not work. These tactics only delayed the day of reckoning, and the Canadian economy had to adjust to higher prices which ultimately gave rise to further problems. The tactics prevented or muted the adjustments to higher efficiency of energy use, which is the normal reaction to price rises.
September 27, 1990

The objective of present policy is to ensure that Canadian energy producers and consumers are free to respond to the pressures and opportunities presented by world markets. We have deregulated oil and natural gas prices. We have sharply reduced oil and natural gas market restrictions, eliminated discriminatory and interventionist tax and incentive measures and reduced the intrusive hand of government in the oil economy. Working more closely with the provinces has helped us create a more stable framework for industry investment. This policy has paid high dividends in terms of industry confidence and improved federal-provincial relations.
The government has no intention of returning to greater industry regulation in the current circumstances. The past has demonstrated that this is not the right approach in dealing with oil market uncertainty.
In normal times our policies lay the basis for both expansion of our resource sector and competitive pricing for consumers. We have intervened primarily to act as a catalyst and investor in certain large energy projects where the national regional economic benefits to be derived are significant and where the costs and risks are so substantial that private investors could not easily cope with them alone.
Our policy has recognized, of course, that we do not always live in normal times. As recent events demonstrate, the world remains vulnerable to oil supply disruptions due to a variety of political and military events that cannot be predicted or controlled.
In November 1974, in response to the oil crisis of the time, 21 of the world's principal industrialized countries signed an agreement on an international energy plan and the International Energy Agency, the IEA, was created. The basic task of the IEA is to reduce the industrialized countries excessive demand on oil in meeting energy requirements and to bring about a better mix of energy supply and demand over the near and long term. These objectives are pursued by setting in place co-operative programs and sound, compatible energy policies.
In times of oil crises, IEA member states have agreed to implement plans to reduce consumption, draw down emergency oil reserves maintained for the purpose and share available oil supplies. The objective is to balance
Government Orders
demand with supply among the member states in order to equitably share the burden of supply losses and minimize adverse economic impacts. In the case of an incipient oil supply crisis, the International Energy Agency governing board can implement co-ordinated emergency response measures which can be taken in creeping crises conditions that remain below the International Energy Agency's emergency trigger level of a 7 per cent reduction of normal supply.
The Coordinated Emergency Response Measures involve voluntary actions that can be taken by member states in a pre-crisis situation. These measures may include use of surge production, stock draw, fuel switching and oil demand restraint. In Canada's case, there are few opportunities for fuel switching and surge production, and Canada is exempt from the IEA's stock holding obligation because of our position as a net oil exporter. Consequently, any action by Canada under this program would have to take the form of demand restraint.
The invoking of the oil sharing system has never been necessary in the past. Other means have been found to deal with oil supply disruptions. If needed, oil sharing would give expression to our collective commitment to security. It is premature, however, to speculate on whether such a system will in fact be needed.
Canada has long had in place an effective emergency planning system. In 1974, the Energy Supplies Allocation Board was set up by the Energy Supplies Emergency Act. The act gave the Energy Supplies Allocation Board the responsibility for preparing and, if necessary, implementing contingency plans during an oil crisis.
The government has not waited to see the results of unfolding events in the Middle East to get its house in order. We have begun acting to prepare for any necessary response should the supply situation deteriorate. Included in the actins we have taken are the following.
We have reviewed the measures that Canada could take in terms of demand restraint, and we have updated the readiness of existing emergency plans under the Emergency Supplies Allocation Board. If there is an oil crisis in Canada, Canada has the power to allocate crude oil and petroleum products. There is also a provision for gasoline and diesel fuel rationing at the retail level, but it

September 27, 1990
Government Orders
would only be implemented in a situation of extreme shortages.
Additionally, federal officials have met with their provincial counterparts to brief them on the International Energy Agency and international oil market developments and to explore what actions could be taken to reduce demands on petroleum supplies.
We are meeting regularly with industry associations and oil company representatives to apprise them of our plans and to facilitate our monitoring of the state of oil product markets within our country.
The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and I, as minister, will be stepping up our efforts over the coming period to reduce oil demand and to work with the provinces on other measures that will have a national impact. An initial meeting with provincial government officials has already been held to discuss a national co-operative initiative that would emphasize increased energy conservation and encourage voluntary restraint of energy demand. These measures will become even more germane as we approach the colder months of late fall and winter.
I am also pleased to report to the House that we have had successful and co-operative sessions with the provinces, including a day-and-a-half meeting in early September to update provincial representatives on developments within the International Energy Agency and on issues concerning international and domestic oil markets. Like the world-wide community itself, the provinces know all too well that this is a global energy problem we have on our hands, not a regional energy problem. It is a problem that goes well beyond provincial boundaries.
I would also like to report to the House that our government is maintaining ongoing contact with the industry throughout this period of oil market uncertainty. We have also had close liaison and information exchanges with our partners in the International Energy Agency. So our lines of communication both domestically and internationally are open at all times. I might mention parenthetically that International Energy Agency countries are meeting tomorrow in Paris to consider measures that may be required to deal with the present situation.
In the meantime, we expect Canadian oil companies not to take advantage of the situation. Companies are already co-operating by providing information on oil
supply and prices. We expect that they will take all measures necessary to ensure continuity of supply and the integrity of the Canadian supply system. We also expect the industry will follow responsible pricing and marketing practices. My officials will be monitoring the situation closely, along with the provinces.
We must recognize, however, that as the situation evolves, prices have and will rise. I give the House this example. In the first quarter of 1989, the average price of oil in Canada was $15 West Texas Intermediate or WTI, before the invasion of Kuwait. That average price had moved by the end of 1989 from $15 to approximately $20 WTI, U.S. At the meetings prior to August 2, the day of the invasion, the meetings of OPEC had brought the price of oil in the order of $21 to $23 WTI. It is that pricing, that increase from the first quarter of 1989, to the pricing prior to the situation in the Middle East that is being reflected in energy price increases today.
Anyone who speculates that the pricing today is already including the effects of the August 2 period and the post-August 2 period is simply not being accurate in terms of analysing the market and the accounting for oil which we have in Canada as distinct from the accounting for oil that the United States uses. I think it is important that we in the House understand that accounting system.
We cannot predict precisely how prices will move in the future. Short of a major supply crisis, price movements are the logical and most effective way balance supply and demand. It is, of course, important that the full competitive forces of the market remain free to operate. Remedies are available under existing competition legislation in the event of demonstrated anti-competitive behaviour.
Mr. Speaker, the present situation is not one that requires drastic or precipitous action. Through our international partners and our own market analysis, we are staying well informed regarding the evolution of the oil market, the likelihood of general or specific shortages and the movement of prices.
It is important, that Canadians realize that the risk of a disruptive situation arising could be reduced and made more manageable if we all were to exercise some extra prudence in our use of energy over the coming months. By using energy more efficiently, deferring uses that are not necessary and conserving available supplies, we can
September 27, 1990

all demonstrate good citizenship and possibly reduce the necessity for more stringent measures later on.
The department will be working closely with the provinces and territories to collaborate on voluntary petroleum demand restraint measures, to co-ordinate plans, particularly in the transportation area and to demonstrate leadership by example. Through the regular meetings of the Interprovincial Advisory Committee on Energy, we will ensure good communications between both levels of government.
Let me conclude, Mr. Speaker, by stating that the situation in the Persian Gulf should remind all of us that we live in a world dominated by uncertainty. What we take for granted today can become tomorrow's great dilemma.
The Government of Canada has responded to these events in the only ways that make sense, through collective action with our international partners, through effective emergency planning and through the continuation of general energy policies that promote the flexibility and growth of the Canadian energy sector.
I think that all Canadians realize and recognize that we face a wide-ranging problem. Isolationism just does not work in this kind of oil crises. In these days of uncertainty, Canada shares a world-wide problem and we have to learn to work and think at a world-wide level. I am confident we can do it, but we must be prepared to accept co-operative and creative measures that will help to entrench a unique kind of common solidarity with the international community.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments. The hon. member for Dartmouth.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great interest to the hon. minister opposite. I found very helpful some of the information he put forward today, particularly as it relates to the energy sector in Canada.
However, I would submit to him-and I do not just want to be taking a cheap shot-that perhaps this is some of the information we could have had a bit earlier if his government opposite had done the right thing when this crisis first jumped on the scene and perhaps had an earlier recall of Parliament.
Government Orders
Some of the issues the hon. minister is talking about now are going to have to be debated much further in the very near future. I have some concerns, and I want to ask the minister what specific plans he and his colleagues and the department have to put in place, if we do indeed find out that there is some unfair pricing because of the current crisis in the gulf.
Everybody knows that in the international energy industry, particularly the oil industry, a multilevel pricing takes place. Then we get sort of a blended price as to what exactly is a fair price, given a particular circumstance at a particular point in time.
Most Canadians do not know whether or not they are paying a fair price, but when they see the price going up at the pumps they have a tendency to believe that somebody is digging a bit too deep into their pockets.
I want the minister, if he is able, to give me, members of the House, and Canadians generally some idea-a glimpse perhaps-of the plans that he and his colleagues in other departments like Consumer and Corporate Affairs have to ensure that they are not just monitoring. I would like to make sure that they have the capability to monitor, but if they are going to be monitoring and if some unfair pricing is taking place, at what point do they put in place a plan of action? How do they roll back the prices? What pressure can they put on those national and international companies that are in the oil industry in Canada?
In particular I look at Atlantic Canada which is susceptible to changing prices at the international level. In Atlantic Canada, but for the announcement the other day and the bill that we now have before this place, there is no oil production. In a few years hence we will have oil production from the Hibernia field, we hope, but at the current time we are basically hostage to energy, to oil from another place.
I have a second question for the minister, because I can only get the floor once and I am interested. I would like to know if the current situation which has threatened our security of supply of oil, of energy in Canada, leads the minister to review the position that his government seems to have abandoned, that is of pursuing a policy of energy self-sufficiency in Canada.
In particular, will the minister do everything he possibly can now that we all know how volatile the Middle East situation is today, and perhaps for years to come,

September 27, 1990
Government Orders
and the effect it can have on our national oil supplies? Will he give some type of commitment today to review, to promote, and to do everything he can to try to get this government to approve the proposal put forward by the Synfuels consortium to take Cape Breton high sulphur coal and, through some fairly unique proven processes, turn it into a synthetic oil product? Can he give us some of those assurances here today?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of questions there. I am not going to eat into the 10 minutes of members opposite unduly.
Let me make a few points, first of all in respect to pricing. The hon. member recognizes in his own question that the matter of pricing and blended price or a world reference price, as it is referred to, is very difficult to determine. Quite frankly-and I have looked very carefully at the fluctuations of oil prices and pump prices- when prices go down we as consumers accept that, as it is time that the market is responding to the needs as we perceive them as consumers. In reverse, when the prices go up there is an easy charge made or a very quick charge made that prices are too high.
I think that also applies, for example, when one takes a look at the price differential between Canadian gasoline and American gasoline. When one takes a look at the present situation, one will find that there is still a price differential even if one takes into account exchange rates and volumes. That primarily and almost totally is the difference in federal and provincial taxes.
Having said that, we will continue monitoring if there is an uncompetitive position. As the hon. member knows, that would have to be done under anti-combines investigations and would have to be done with a legitimate due process which has been passed into law by this House.
Second, in terms of Atlantic Canada, the hon. member makes a very valid point. At the present time-and I take one area of departure from him-the Government of Canada has not abandoned self-sufficiency in oil and in energy. In fact quite the opposite. The whole basis of our energy policy at the present time is just to stay with oil and oil products.
Canada exported in the last quarter, on average, approximately 275,000 barrels a day in crude and in oil products. It is for that reason I mentioned that we as an exporter were not subject to the strategic oil reserves of the International Energy Agency to which other countries like the United States, for example, are subject.
Having said that, on the east coast we are importing about 550,000 barrels a day, about 350,000 from the North Sea. That is why I parted company with a number of my colleagues yesterday when they said, for example, that if the oil from the Hibernia oil fields were to go to the United States, why should it not go to Canadian refineries?
On the surface it is a very easy question, and the answer seems to be even as straightforward as the question. The fact of the matter is that because of our distribution system on the east coast through Portland, Maine, we need those 550,000 barrels from offshore as the hon. member put forward. In terms of energy self-sufficiency, that is why we are doing Hibernia.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted a clarification from the minister. I have been getting a number of calls and letters-and I am sure he has as well-with regard to the increased prices at the gas pumps. If I have understood his remarks correctly, he is saying that whatever has happened just recently at the gas pumps is in fact not related to the Kuwait crisis.
Certainly those constituents of mine with whom I have spoken believe that what is happening is that the reserves that were accumulated are still being sold. They do not understand that the prices should increase. Perhaps he can just inform me a bit so I can talk with my constituents.
The other questions are two very brief ones. Normally before we enter a conflict such as this one-and it might have been a more appropriate question for the Minister of National Defence-there are briefings given to the ministers and to cabinet. One question that would normally be asked is: What is the probability of conflict when we send a force to such a situation? Obviously some estimates are given. Of course, if there were a conflict, do we have a sense of the estimates of possible law of supply?
September 27, 1990

Is the minister at all in a position to inform me and this House of those particular questions? I would appreciate that.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the last question, I am not in a position to answer that one.
In terms of briefings, I have offered briefings to critics opposite. A number of them have taken up that offer. I understand that will be done next week.
Specifically with reference to the member's question- and this gets into what is known as oil accounting-I will try to be as succinct as I can be. I mentioned to the hon. member that over approximately the last year and a half the price of oil on a reference of West Texas Intermediate, WTI, we have seen an increase of about $15 to $20 to approximately slightly higher prior to the August 2 invasion.
There is a time lag between when that crude has been bought and is sold at the gasoline pump, which varies somewhat from region to region in Canada depending on refinery capacity and storage capacity. Generally speaking, we can look at somewhere between 60 days and 75 days. That will vary from region to region slightly. Having said that, oil that was purchased has come through the system and we are seeing the reflection of that higher energy price at the pumps now. What we have not yet seen at the pumps are the possible increases because of the crisis in the Persian Gulf.
That is why I mentioned the August 2 date very specifically as being the next reference point and, if present prices continue, consumers will see an increase in prices beyond the present level.

Mr. Speaker, I understand in Washington the joke on the Persian Gulf crisis goes: "Why did we go in there? Oh, we went in there on principle. Do you spell it p-a-1 or 1-e? And the answer is you spell it o-i-1, oil". This is an oil war in many ways.
I am glad the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has spoken on this matter. I just want to tell him that what Canadians are concerned about is that the prices have not gone up as a result of the Persian Gulf. We think in Vancouver they have. Canadians are concerned that if the world price goes down it takes a long time to work its way through the system to the pump, but
Government Orders
when it goes up it seems like overnight the prices go up. We are concerned about whether there is any regulation to that.
The competition bureau is a toothless tiger. What the government should be doing is putting in place-and I ask it to consider this-a better mechanism to look at the increase in prices so that there will not be windfall profits if there are actually further difficulties with oil prices as a result of the more serious difficulties, if that is possible, in the Persian Gulf.
I think the minister should consider looking at that matter. The other thing I want to ask the minister just briefly is: Has he considered that maybe the Conservative government should reverse its policy on energy? We were moving toward energy self-sufficiency, to Canadian control. Now we have sold our oil and gas to the Americans in this big free market, with the United States in this free trade deal. Does the Persian Gulf situation not show us that we now are at risk? I do not think we were at risk. I think if we had developed our own energy resources through Petro-Canada and through Canadian companies, not through Mobil and Hibernia or by ignoring the other development, then we could have been protected from this crisis.
We have this energy in Canada. We have the oil and gas. Why are we still dependent on the Persian Gulf and have put ourselves in that position? Have the government's policies not led to this dependency?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I tried to make plain to the hon. member, In fact quite the opposite has happened. We are a net exporter of oil. We are energy self-sufficient in almost every form. In fact, in many areas we are world leaders and world suppliers. One that he does not much appreciate is uranium. We are also energy self-sufficient; we now have our gas bubble. Our problem is one of transportation systems. Our problem is one of infrastructure to bring more to the market.
With respect to oil and oil products, we are at a net value today per day, exporting 275,000 barrels per day more than, for example, we need for our own production. On the question of self-sufficiency, the issue is different from the one he raises about Canadianization.
I want to give him a reference, and I will be very brief. I took a look at what the National Energy Program was projecting the price of oil would be this week, and I just

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CRIMINAL CODE FIREARMS ACQUISITION CERTIFICATE
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   CRIMINAL CODE FIREARMS ACQUISITION CERTIFICATE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should initiate amendments to Part III of the Criminal Code (Firearms) to provide:
1)	That a "Firearms Acquisition Certificate" be required for the purchase of ammunition;
2)	That there be a mandatory two-week delay between the application for a "Firearms acquisition Certificate" and the actual granting of the "Certificate".
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion is part of a two-track approach to tighten gun laws in Canada. This particular motion would amend the Criminal Code to provide that a firearms acquisition certificate must be used in order to obtain ammunition as well as a new firearm, and I will explain the reason for that. The motion also proposes that there be a mandatory two-week waiting period between the application for a firearms acquisition certificate and the actual granting of that certificate.
I said that this motion is part of a two-track approach. I also have on the Order Paper a private member's bill, Bill C-283, which I introduced on February 2, 1990. That
bill also demands that the firearms acquisition certificate be necessary for the purchase of ammunition and provides for the two-week delay in obtaining a firearms acquisition certificate. But in addition, the bill requires that the application for the firearms acquisition certificate be accompanied by the signatures of two citizens attesting to the responsibility of the applicant. It also provides that the firearms acquisition certificate be only good for two years rather than five years, so that the police have an opportunity to investigate the applicant on a more regular basis.
I should point out that in the horrible massacre of the 16 women in Montreal in 1989, the killer had a firearms acquisition certificate. However, it was an old one that he had had for several years and his degenerated state of mind had not been subject to examination or to scrutiny over that period of time. I have also proposed, and it is not in this motion, that such weapons as the STRUM semi-automatic rifle, which was used in the Ecole polytechnique massacre, should be placed on the restricted weapon list.
I repeat that this motion, and my bill which is on the Order Paper, were presented to the House of Commons in the aftermath of the December 6, 1989 massacre at the Ecole polytechnique. However, I go on to advise the House that I have been a long-standing proponent of tough gun laws. I have had bills and motions on the Order Paper and debated in this House for more than 20 years. When I was Solicitor General I took steps to tighten our gun laws and that was done while I was a minister in government.
I must say that while advances were made at that time, I was never completely satisfied and incidents since that time have shown that my gut feelings with respect to what was done was correct. The incident at the University of Montreal, the Ecole polytechnique, demonstrated that the laws that we now have, while much tougher than those the United States, are still not adequate.
I would like to briefly describe the present regime for gun controls in Canada. We have three classifications of guns. First of all we have prohibited weapons, which are not permitted to ordinary citizens under any circumstances. These are fully automatic weapons such as machine guns and sawed-off shotguns which can only be used for criminal purposes. Well, prohibited weapons are
September 27, 1990

not allowed for sale to the public but may only be used by the armed forces and by the police.
The next category is restricted weapons. Restricted weapons are hand guns, revolvers and so on and semiautomatic weapons. A person may obtain a restricted weapon for one of five reasons. I will not go into the reasons now but these reasons are set down in the law. You apply for the use of a restricted weapon such as a hand gun, for example, if you are a private detective. That is one of the reasons you may get a permit and obtain a restricted weapon.
Finally, we have what I call regulated weapons. These are ordinary long guns such as rifles and shotguns which are used for hunting and other sporting purposes. These are permitted for sale to the public as long as you have a firearms acquisition certificate when you purchase them. For a long time these guns were subject to no regulation whatsoever.
As a matter of fact, when I first came to Parliament, I can recall a very well-known incident where a young man went to a sporting goods store here on Sparks Street. He was very disturbed, went in and bought a shotgun and took the shotgun to his high school, opened the door and started firing on the class, killing several students and the teacher. This young man was able to buy that shotgun without any questions asked, as if he were buying a package of bubblegum.
It was in the aftermath of that incident that we brought in the firearms acquisition certificate. Now, in order to purchase a long gun, an ordinary rifle or shotgun you need a firearms acquisition certificate and there is a certain investigation before you can get it.
However, there are still many inadequacies and shortcomings in the law. For example, although we have the firearms acquisition certificate, in the present law there is no mandatory delay between the application and the granting of the certificate.
We had an incident in Montreal where a woman, in an extremely emotional situation because she found her husband was fooling around with another woman, went to a sporting goods store to buy a shotgun. When she was told she needed the firearms acquisition certificate, she went to the police and applied in the morning and got the certificate in the afternoon.
Private Members' Business
The present law says that there should be an investigation by the police, but there is no mandatory delay. She applied in the morning, got the gun in the afternoon and went to her husband's place of business and shot him. That sort of incident demonstrated that a mandatory delay is a reasonable proposal, a reasonable addition, to these laws.
Since I tabled this motion and since I tabled Bill C-283, the government has come forward with legislation. I congratulate the government for Bill C-80 because it does deal with some of the proposals that I have been pushing for many years. For example, it provides for a mandatory delay of 28 days and I think that is a very good measure.
It also provides for one of the other provisions that I have in my bill. I propose that every applicant for a firearms acquisition certificate must have the countersignatures of two citizens in his or her community attesting to the responsibility of the applicant. We do that, by the way, with passport applications. You have to get your passport countersigned by one of a list of people who will certify that you are the person you claim to be.
The minister has stated in Bill C-80 that every applicant will require two references. He or she will also need a photograph to go along with the application which will be on the firearms acquisition certificate. That is not the case now. I think this is an additional protection.
Mr. Speaker, the bill does not go far enough. If we are going to amend Canadian gun laws, I believe we should do it right once and for all. For example, one major gap in the law at the present time is that the firearms acquisition certificate is only required for the purchase of new weapons, it does not apply to all those long guns that have been hanging around in the homes of families on the shelves for years and years.
To cover that situation I have proposed that the firearms acquisition certificate should be required whenever an individual purchases ammunition. I do not see any great problem with that. If you already have a firearms acquisition certificate, you would simply show it when you went to purchase ammunition. This means that you would throw an obstacle in the way of those people who might wish to use a weapon under severe emotional circumstances, a weapon that they might borrow, a weapon that they might have had in the family for a long

Private Members' Business
time. I think that would be a good measure and would not cause too much inconvenience to the law-abiding citizen who wants to go hunting or participate in sport shooting.
By the way, the other thing that should go into the government bill is a shorter renewal period. I refer again to the massacre at the Ecole polytechnique. It is possible that someone at the age of 18 might apply for a firearms acquisition certificate and have a good reputation in the community at that time and have no blemish on his or her record. But if you wait for five years for a renewal, a lot of things can happen.
For example, we have to renew our automobile licences every one or two years. If your record declines considerably in that period of time then you are refused your licence. As a matter of fact you can lose your licence with demerit marks even during the period that you hold the licence.
While I congratulate the government for what is in Bill C-80, I would hope that it would consider the amendments which are contained in my motion before the House and in my bill which is also before the House.
Why do we propose these kinds of laws? There is a very large lobby in Canada opposed to any type of gun law. They have the feeling that we are trying to prevent the law-abiding citizen from having guns which they would use for legitimate purposes such as hunting and sport shooting. Well, that is not the case at all. I have used the analogy over and over again with other activities that we take part in, in life.
No one would think for a moment that because we required the licensing of automobiles and the licensing of chauffeurs and drivers of automobiles that we are trying to restrict legitimate use of automobiles. Not at all. What we are trying to do when we require the testing of people who apply for an automobile licence is to make sure that those who get those licences are responsible people who drive their cars properly and know the rules of the road.
Surely, a gun which was designed and manufactured to kill, whether it be killing an animal in hunting or to kill in war or for the police to protect communities, the purpose of the gun is to kill. If we have licences and registration for automobiles, then surely we should have them for guns. I think this country has accepted that principle for a long time. We have accepted the principle
and now it is simply a question of tightening up, of closing the loopholes, closing the gaps so that we make it more complete. But we do not. I have never had any intention of keeping guns away from law-abiding hunters and sport shooters. Canada has had a great record in Olympic sport shooting and international competitions. That is not our goal.
The opponents of stricter gun laws say that if you ban guns, and of course we are not proposing that we ban guns, only criminals will have guns. You see that slogan on bumper stickers and on posters and so on. I must point out that two-thirds of the homicides in Canada are committed under severe emotional circumstances, usually by family members and acquaintances. Most homicides in Canada are not committed by the so-called professional killers. The people who attempt to get guns under severe circumstances are people that usually have never committed a crime before in their lives. It is at those people that we direct our gun laws.
I know that we will never stop homicide altogether. We will have a very difficult time keeping guns out of the hands of the professional criminal, the so-called gangster. They will always find a way to get guns. But two-thirds of our murders are not committed by gangsters or professional killers. They are committed by husband against wife, or by a group of friends who get in an argument over one thing or another, usually with alcohol or drugs involved. Mr. Speaker, it is those people, if you look at the statistics and the records, who look for a gun when they get extremely angry and upset. It is toward them that we formulate these laws.
Again, the opponents of these laws say that we should not put in restrictive measures-what I would call preventive measures-but let us rely on tougher penalties. We know that, while tougher penalties may be one way of approaching the problem, it is not the best way. It is applying the tough penalty after the crime has been committed, the murder has been done. Is it not better to prevent the crime from taking place?
If we had prevented that young man from getting that gun last year at the Ecole polytechnique, those 16 women might still be alive today. There was the case that took place in Ottawa several years ago. If that young man had not got that shotgun that day, those murders may not have taken place. That is why the mandatory delay, which is in my motion and in the government bill, is a
September 27, 1990

Private Members' Business
good thing. Very often the emotional crisis that the individual is undergoing could very well disappear after a week, 15 days, or two weeks. Lots of things could happen to cool the person down. Even though the individual might have applied for a firearm's acquisition certificate in the hope of getting a gun, first, the police might turn down the application, but second, the circumstances might very well have changed after 28 days.
The gangster or the professional criminal will always get guns. But if we can reduce the number of murders committed with guns by those who are not professional criminals, and that is the large number in Canada, if we can even reduce them by 50 or 100 a year, we will be accomplishing something. I suggest that the House might very well do that.
I want to point out that after we tightened the gun laws in 1978 there was a considerable decline in the rate of crime with guns in the country. The facts are on the record. For the countries of the world with strict gun laws, the rate of crime with guns is much lower than those countries with loose gun laws.
The most flagrant example is the United States where the gun laws for the most part are state laws because the criminal law in the United States is a state responsibility rather than national. The rate of crime with guns in the United States is considerably higher than in Canada and considerably higher than in those countries that have strict gun laws. The most recent statistic is that in the United States 60 per cent of homicides are committed with guns where in Canada only one-third of homicides are committed with guns.
Mr. Speaker, you indicate to me that I have only one minute left. I will just deal in that one minute with another slogan that is put forward by those that lobby against stricter gun laws. The slogan goes that people kill, not guns. Well, of course, people kill and the guns do not kill all by themselves, but it has been demonstrated that guns have been five times more effective in killing than any other weapon, for example, a knife. That is obvious to anyone that knows anything about guns. A gun is an effective way of killing and surely we should do something to keep guns out of the hands of those who are irresponsible, who have a record of alcoholism, mental instability, family violence and so on. These are the people at whom we aim our tougher guns laws.
While I congratulate the government for Bill C-80, I would hope that the ideas that are put forward in this debate will provide it with some thought and perhaps will lead to some amendment of Bill C-80 when we approach that bill later on so that it can be made even a more effective bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today in response to the motion of the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace in which the government is asked to initiate the following amendments to Part III of the Criminal Code: first, require a firearms acquisition certificate at the time of purchase of munitions; and second, impose a mandatory two-week delay between the application for a firearms acquisition certificate and the actual granting of the certificate.
Before I go any further, however, I would like to say the hon. member is to be commended for his sustained interest in this aspect of the law. The House will recall that the hon. member played a major role in the proceedings leading up to the passage of the gun control provisions now in effect.
According to certain studies, the percentage of deaths related to the use of firearms is so much lower in Canada than in the United States because of the strict gun control provisions we have in the Criminal Code today. For instance, perhaps I may draw your attention to the special article that appeared on November 1988, in the New England Journal of Medicine, on the impact of handgun regulations in two cities that are very similar, namely Seattle and Vancouver.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians must never forget the date of December 6, 1989, when Marc Lepine, a young man in his early twenties, entered the Ecole polytechnique of the University of Montreal around 5:20 p.m., carrying a semi-automatic .223 caliber Ruger Mini-14, and killed fourteen young women before turning his weapon on himself and taking his own life.
This, the worst killing in Canada's history, caused considerable consternation among the people of Quebec and Canadians in general.

Private Members' Business
Subsequently, it was found that in this particular case, the application for a firearms acquisition certificate had been made on September 5,1989, and that the certificate was granted several days later.
Apparently, there was nothing unusual about the way the Quebec authorities processed the application. A routine investigation failed to produce a police record or any other information that would justify rejecting the application. Lepine purchased the firearm on November 21, 1989, with 100 bullets and two secondhand magazines.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, Bill C-80, an Act to amend the Criminal Code and the Customs Thriff in consequence thereof, was tabled in the House of Commons by the Minister of Justice on June 26, 1990.
This bill contains several provisions that reflect the public's growing concern about violence related to the use of firearms. The government's tabling of Bill C-80 would seem appropriate at this time, to deal with the problem of gun control in Canada. I regret, however that I cannot support the hon. member's motion as such, although I appreciate his motives.
Canadian firearms legislation has always tried to strike a balance between the rights of bona fide, legitimate users and the safety of the Canadian public. This also applies to the proposals tabled in the House.
The amendments proposed in Bill C-80 are the result of long consultation with sports and firearms associations, police corps, public interest groups and provincial authorities.
Hunters, target shooters and collectors have for many years been allowed to own and use firearms, and the proposed legislation is not intended to prevent them from doing so.
Furthermore, regarding the waiting period suggested by the hon. member in his motion, I may point out that the period provided in the bill is twice as long.
Mr. Speaker, the proposed amendments are intended to give the public better protection by improving the screening procedure for applications for firearms acquisition certificates. Furthermore, the Minister of Justice has announced the government's intention to proclaim the coming into effect of a provision of the Criminal Code enacted in 1977, under which persons applying for a firearms acquisition certificate would have to establish that they have either finished a course or passed a test on
the safe handling and use of firearms, before obtaining the certificate. Both course and test must be approved by the Attorney General of the province concerned. However, the provinces have yet to ratify the coming into effect of this provision.
Course content will be established in consultation with the provincial authorities and with the assistance of the Canadian advisory council on firearms. The government, working together with the provinces, will set up a national training program to encourage safe handling and use of firearms. The minister has also announced that the firearms acquisition certificate will be revised to include the owner's photograph.
The requirement that the certificate must be produced when ammunition is purchased would substantially alter the original purpose of the certificate, which was to ensure that individuals who acquire firearms are not a danger to society. The hon. member's proposal would, to a certain extent, have the effect of making the certificate of acquisition a certificate of ownership. I think this is one aspect of the question that could appropriately be considered when Bill C-80 is referred to a legislative committee after second reading.
I am looking forward to further discussion at second reading of the amendments proposed in the bill, in the not too distant future.

Again it made us look seriously at our gun control legislation in Canada. I should point out at the time of that happening my colleague, the member for


September 27, 1990

Saanich-Gulf Islands, said in the House and I will quote from her comments on December 11. She said:
Mr. Speaker, today in Montreal thousands of women are mourning the deaths of 14 women at the hands of a gun-toting madman. He was able to buy his semi-automatic rifle because he had met all legal requirements.
On Saturday, the Prime Minister said the ease with which Marc Lepine obtained his instrument of mass murder was "serious and unacceptable". He is quoted as saying his government would deal with the problem if necessary.

Non-restricted weapons, FACs as they are called, are rather simple to obtain. Depending on the province and where you live, you can obtain one within a few hours, or a few weeks if it involves the mail. The body responsible in the province for granting the FAC does a check of criminal records involving violent crime and mental illness involving violence. Although it is rarely an indepth investigation, there is no problem, the FAC is granted.
It is more difficult to obtain restricted weapons, as you might expect. As I said, individuals who obtained weapons before 1978 and have not obtained a weapon since do not need to have FACs.
I will deal first with part two of the motion. The motion calls for a mandatory two-week delay between the application of an FAC and a granting of the licence. The idea, I gather, is to ensure a cooling off period to stop individuals from buying guns on impulse, as the hon.
Private Members' Business
member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace outlined a few cases about this, and the individuals using the gun.
I noticed the member proposed in his motion two weeks. The government bill, Bill C-80, asked for a delay of 28 days. That would make his motion less onerous than the government bill. He says the government bill is better. We will get to consider that I believe in Bill C-80 in committee, and that is one matter we should look at.
Part one of this motion today is the more controversial element of the motion. As it states, it would require that individuals have an FAC to obtain ammunition. This would have several important effects. On the positive side, it would ensure that those who had obtained a weapon illegally would have difficulty getting ammunition without an FAC. On the other hand, we might as well acknowledge this, it would not in fact affect those people who have had a gun before 1978 and do not need to have an FAC. So in a sense, it is retroactive legislation, although indirect if you like retroactive legislation, but it has a retroactive effect nevertheless. That is something that this committee has to consider and consider veiy carefully because it potentially applies to hundreds of thousands of people in the country. I want to deal with that controversial matter.
I have just become justice critic for my party. I have looked at my mail and I see many letters. Here is a letter from a Mr. Jarvis in North Vancouver who writes to me and says he thinks Bill C-80 is unfair because it really does not succeed in hitting those people who misuse guns and it hits the people, the hunters, and others who are law-abiding citizens. You get that view expressed widely. The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace dealt with that in his speech.
Here is another view from one of my constituents, Miss Elizabeth Thunstrom. Her view is the opposite. She points out that she is very much is favour of more restriction when it comes to firearms, so you have a divided public on this matter. I personally think that the people of Canada are in favour of gun control, accept gun control and want workable gun control.
I am told that there is a difference between people who live in rural areas and those who live in urban areas. For example, trappers, guides and outfitters use guns as tools. If an outfitter goes on a canoe trip, drops his gun, drops his ammunition and has to get more, the question

September 27, 1990
Private Members' Business
is: does he have to wait two weeks or 28 days or so on in order to get another check or another firearms acquisition certificate? These are real issues for a group of people and we have to find a way that we can make this thing workable.
I personally feel that it is in the long-term interest of those who legally possess guns in Canada, hunters, trappers, gun collectors and people who have a legitimate interest in guns, to have proper gun control as well. I believe that with some thought, in committee we can bridge the gap here. It may be that we have to work out a system in our country where the municipalities could have some control so, for instance, in metropolitan Toronto it would be very difficult to get a permit for guns or ammunition whereas in the municipality of Prince Rupert it might be a lot easier, in the sense that there are more people who are trapping and hunting for a living in Prince Rupert. That is just a thought and that will have to be considered at the committee.
Again, I support the motion in principle. I believe that we can deal with some of these matters in detail when the legislation hits the legislative committee.
Finally, I would like to say that we should compare our situation in Canada with that of the United States. In Canada, we consistently have had stronger gun laws than the Americans. I think the result of this is partly responsible for the fact that we have less violence in our society. In general, each time we strengthen gun laws we do succeed in limiting the illegal use of firearms in Canada. I believe tougher gun control laws are overwhelmingly supported by Canadians, especially when we contrast them with the American situation, with the one caveat that we try to find a less onerous and bureaucratic way for those people who are in rural areas or who use guns in the course of their work, as is the case for trappers and guides.
As the Ecole polytechnique tragedy shows, we cannot become complacent. As we have suggested before and after the tragedy, our laws can and must be strengthened and made to work better. I look forward to seeing Bill C-80 in committee and look forward to finding ways that we can make this legislation workable and that we can continue, as the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace said, to in fact make Canada a safer society and
that we can focus our gun laws so that we are looking at that group of people which he said committed the two-thirds of homicides that were not committed by professional killers but by people in trouble; in family situations often times, disturbed people, the Lepines of this world.

It was the night of a Christmas party, a night when a number of members of Parliament were getting together before we would all return to our ridings. Late in the evening, we were joined by our colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte. When he entered the room, I could tell that something terrible had happened. He told us of the appalling events, the massacre of the 16 young women at the Ecole polytechnique. I remember the comment of another colleague at that point who said: "Things like that do not happen in Canada".
I recall again the next day when all of us on all sides of this House were united in sorrow and in mourning for the death of these young women. We all felt that way, that things like this do not happen in Canada. Indeed, we used to enjoy that belief and that certainty that things like this did not happen in Canada. Unfortunately, that is no longer the case.
I certainly have no wish to denigrate in any way the appalling tragedy of the Ecole polytechnique, but violence
September 27, 1990

has become a common thing in our country, most particularly in our cities. I am sorry to say, in my own city of Halifax where violent crime was practically non-existent when I was growing up, the incidents of murder by guns has increased substantially and, with that, an increase in death by firearms.
There comes, whether we really are aware of it on the surface or not, a hardening of attitude. Along with that are the rapid changes in our culture. I refer particularly to the kinds of television and film that we are exposed to. What is happening is that we are becoming desensitized to the issue of guns. We are becoming desensitized to the sight of people being killed or maimed by firearms.
Now I am not, by any means, suggesting that Canadians are not moved and are not disturbed greatly by this change in our own attitude. I am not suggesting that Canadians are totally insensitive or even past, if you will, the 50 per cent line of sensitivity on the issue of gun control and access to guns. What I am saying is that we are farther down the road than we were even half a generation ago. I want to make very clear that, as my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace said earlier, I am not attempting to prevent hunters or sports shooters in this country from access to their use of firearms in a well trained, law-abiding manner.
I have spoken to lobby groups in my own riding. I have spoken to national lobby groups as well. I am not particularly keen on firearms at all. I will be perfectly honest. They make me nervous. However, I know there are lots of people, women and men in this country, who are expert in the use of firearms and in whose possession they will be used for their correct purpose. These are not the situations we need worry about.
When I think of Marc Lepine, when I think of those young women in Montreal, when I think that tonight in every major city in Canada many women and children will be menaced by firearms, because it is happening on a daily basis, when I think that our gradual desensitization to the whole issue of violence is becoming more and more the norm and less and less the exception, and when I remember those young women who died and I know that every day in this country women are dying from violent crime, then I say we cannot merely do the adequate. We must push beyond that to the ultimate and ensure that our gun control legislation is the finest in the

world, that our gun control legislation offers the kind of protection that Canadians deserve.
I have heard frequently from people who oppose gun control the rather nauseating phrase that suggests that people who are in favour of gun control are a bit dull, that guns do not kill people; people kill people. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace has proposed that the government make certain changes to the gun control provisions of the Criminal Code. He wants to require a firearms acquisition certificate for the purchase of ammunition, and he wants a mandatory two-week delay between the application for an FAC and the time at which it is issued to the applicant.
As most members of this House will be aware, the Minister of Justice has tabled Bill C-80, an act to amend the Criminal Code and the Customs Tariff in consequence thereof, in this House since the hon. member introduced his motion.
Bill C-80 contains extensive changes to the law of gun control in Canada and is supplemented by a number of non-legislative measures. Canada's gun control law is based on three basic elements. First, it seeks to deter those who would misuse firearms through specific firearms offences and penalties. Second, it seeks to restrict or prohibit access to certain types of firearms believed to be a greater than average threat to public safety. Third, it
seeks to screen out those persons who should not have access to guns and deny them that access.
The firearms acquisition certificate, or FAC, is a key part of the screening process. All Canadians who wish to acquire a gun in any manner, whether by purchase, loan, gift, or even inheritance, must first undergo the necessary screening process and get an FAC.
It is an offence for anyone to give a firearm to any person without proof that the recipient of the gun is a holder of a valid FAC, and it is an offence for any person to obtain a gun unless he or she is the holder of a valid up-to-date FAC.
The legislative and regulatory package recently put forward by the Minister of Justice seeks to improve the FAC in a number of ways. First, it would require those who want an FAC to pass a course or test in firearms safety. Second, it would require them to provide the names of two references who could provide the police firearms officer with additional background information. Third, it would require them to provide an up-to-date photograph that would be attached to the FAC so that unauthorized use would become impossible. Fourth, it would require the applicant wait at least 28 days between the application and receiving his or her FAC. This is double the delay period proposed by my colleague.
As any member of this House who has recently obtained a firearm will be aware, it generally takes at least two weeks for the police to process an application. This delay is not mandatory. It is simply the time required to conduct the necessary check and fill out the forms.
The four-week delay proposed in the minister's bill would significantly lighten the existing wait, and it would ensure a more or less uniform wait as most applications could be dealt with properly in a month. It would also ensure that an FAC was not used in less than a month, even in cases where the paperwork was completed in less time than that.
The Minister of Justice has said that this waiting period is intended to allow firearms officers time to conduct a proper background check, but it seems to me that it will also reduce firearms incidents for another reason. It seems to me that where a person wants to obtain a firearm to commit a crime or perhaps to commit suicide, a one-month delay might well force that person
September 27, 1990

to reconsider. It might in some cases force that person to reflect on the implications of their acts to the point where they decide not to act at all.
For this reason I would support the idea behind this part of the motion. It is a good idea and worthy of support in this House. I am sure that this is why the Minister of Justice has included a similar proposal in her bill, and I am sure the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace will want to support the minister's bill for that reason.
The hon. member has made another proposal in his motion. He has proposed that the same FAC document be required for purchasing ammunition for any firearm. Unfortunately I cannot support this proposal. I believe that it would cause many problems for the police and others involved in the FAC process, and I cannot see any advantages if any exist at all. I am afraid I cannot see any advantage that it would bring in terms of reduced crime, accidents, suicides, or any of the firearms related problems that exist in our country today.
It seems to me that one of the advantages of our present FAC system is that it concentrates on those persons who we think are the greatest risk as firearms owners, those who have just acquired or are about to acquire their guns.
You do not need an FAC to keep a gun. You only need one to acquire a gun. Once you have had the gun for a length of time and have not committed a crime or had an accident with it, I would think that the chances of such an incident ought to drop considerably.
Persons who obtain a gun sometimes do so intending to use it for a crime, and persons who are new gun owners and are not familiar with guns ought to be much more likely to have accidents with them.
I would suggest that this is why the FAC system concentrates its efforts on these people. It concentrates the scarce resources of the police firearms authorities on those situations where we hope they will do the most good.
What then would be the effect of our colleague's proposal? It would force any gun owner who wants to shoot his gun to have an FAC so as to be able to buy ammunition. It would presumably make anyone who sold or even gave ammunition to another person into a criminal unless a valid FAC certificate was presented.
Adjournment Debate
Many Canadians who have owned firearms for years without any problem whatsoever have no FAC. They may have had the guns since before 1978 when an FAC requirement became law, or they may have bought a gun since then using an FAC and not renewed or replaced it.
There is no need to get another FAC to keep a gun you already have. You only need an FAC if you want to get another gun. The hon. member's proposal would change this. He would require the FAC to buy ammunition. He would require those gun owners who have owned their guns without any problems to undergo the FAC screening process regularly.
He would subject them to a more intensive screening process than is contained in the minister's bill. He would force police authorities who must conduct the screening to screen them over and over again, consuming time and resources that could be better used to conduct more effective screening of new gun owners who pose a much greater risk to the public and even to themselves.
I am afraid I cannot support this part of my colleague's motion. I recognize the hon. member's good intentions in putting it forward, but I am afraid that I see it as unworkable and potentially harmful to the existing gun control system and I cannot support it for that reason.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in today's debate. I hope that, once and for all, the Conservative govern-

Adjournment Debate
ment will explain why it insists on misleadingly advertising the GST.
Mr. Speaker, I want to sum up the question I asked in the House last June 1. In short, I wanted to know why the government would not withdraw the GST advertising which I described as being misleading. The Minister of National Revenue told me, and I quote: "I simply want to add for the interest of the hon. member and all members in this House that the GST is not a new tax, even in the service sector".

I read further. On that day, the minister answered questions about the false and misleading advertising of his government. He said:
Mr. Speaker, we analyzed these ads very carefully prior to making them public, particularly after the Speaker's ruling some months ago about another ad of which the hon. member is well aware.
What happened is that the government was telling us that the radio ads of the Conservative government were not false and misleading. We are talking now about the radio ads.
These "spots" as they are called in radio language, had been featured across Canada and Mr. Paul Tuz of the Greater Toronto Better Business Bureau had complained about them to the CRTC.
Mr. Speaker, you know me. Sometimes I decide to take up these challenges myself as well, so I decided to write a letter to the Canadian Advertising Foundation.
I said to myself: "In the unlikely event that someone thinks that I am not totally objective about this thing," which probably would not be the case anyway, but in the event that they said that, I said: "I will let an independent arbitrator be the judge."
"The Advertising Standards Council of the Canadian Advertising Foundation sounds to me to be pretty objective, at least more objective than the Minister of National Revenue." Listen to what they had to say. They wrote to me on August 2, 1990. They said:
Dear Mr. Boudria:
The Canadian Advertising Foundation has followed up on your complaint concerning Government of Canada advertising of the Goods and Services Tax.
It said the following in addition:
The Standards Division of the Canadian Advertising Foundation wrote to the Minister of Finance on June 13, 1990 to advise of the complaints received about this advertising and to inform the Department that the complaints and the advertising in question would be the subject to a review by the Advertising Standards Council at a meeting on July 19, 1990.
On that date, the Advertising Standards Council did indeed review the material to determine compliance with the Canadian Code of Advertising Standards.
I invite the hon. parliamentary secretary opposite to pay close attention to the following sentence. It reads as follows:
The Council ruled that two of the spots entitled "Future" and "The Consumer" to be in violation of Clause 1 of the Canadian Code of Advertising Standards.
Clearly, an independent body has ruled that my complaint was right and that the minister's answer on July 1 was wrong.
I invite the parliamentary secretaiy to tell us now whether he thinks the Canadian Advertising Foundation, the Advertising Standards Council and 85 per cent of Canadians are wrong and that his minister was right.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Reid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague opposite for giving me the opportunity to reply.
The hon. member from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell has expressed concern about, as he terms it, "the $14 million advertising campaign to promote the dreaded GST". Before addressing the member's concerns, I would like to point out that the cost of radio and newspaper advertising in May and June on the GST was about $3.5 million.
As pointed out in the hon. member's question, Mr. Paul Tuz, President of the Better Business Bureau of Metropolitan Toronto, asked the CRTC to remove the government's current radio advertisements from the airwaves because one line was felt to be misleading, and I quote: "It" being the GST "is not an additional tax".
The Better Business Bureau argues that services are not currently subject to a federal sales tax but will be taxed under the GST system. The GST is therefore viewed by the Better Business Bureau as an additional tax on services and not a replacement tax.
September 27, 1990

This argument seems relatively simple and complete. It demonstrates, however, a complete lack of knowledge of the current federal sales tax system because services are taxed indirectly today through business inputs. Many service industries purchase manufactured goods such as computer systems, office equipment, cars, trucks, gasoline and alcoholic beverages, all of which have federal sales tax embedded in their price.
The service sector currently pays an 11 per cent federal sales tax on most telecommunications charges. These taxes invariably are not paid by the businesses but are passed on to the consumers. A percentage of the $700 of federal sales tax collected from each Canadian every year is collected indirectly through the service sector. Although the tax base for the GST will be broadened to ensure a more equitable system, the government is expected to raise net revenues of about $18.5 billion. This represents about the same amount the current federal sales tax would have raised had it remained in place.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: It's revenue neutral, right?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
I will read that again, Mr. Speaker. Although the tax base for the GST will be broadened to ensure a more equitable system, the government is expected to raise net revenues of about $18.5 billion. This represents about the same amount the current federal sales tax would have raised had it remained in place.
In light of these facts, it is clear that the GST is not an additional tax. It is a replacement tax.
The radio advertisements in May and June were factual and straightforward. They were designed to correct the misconceptions demonstrated by the Better Business Bureau of Toronto and, if I may say, the hon. member.
The government has received 360,000 calls on a toll-free information line.
Mr. Speaker, I see you urging me to complete.
Since the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell has posed his question in the House, this issue of the government's radio ads has received further attention. On August 27, 1990, we responded to the Canadian Advertising Foundation. I am happy, either to lay on the table of the House or to give my hon. colleague a copy of
Adjournment Debate
the statement issued at the time and a letter that accompanied it.
